stories.episodeTitle: A Beagle Scout Prepares / Teach a Bird to Fish
stories.situation: Snoopy learns Beagle Scout headquarters is ready to dissolve his troop over zero badges earned, ever, and gives him until the end of summer to turn it around.
stories.coping: Snoopy turns panic into a plan: the Beagle Scout manual reframes the challenge as a chance to shine, and he commits to earning badges one step at a time once camp starts.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: script adds the end-of-summer deadline, the zero-badges reveal and Snoopy's running-in-circles panic beat the synopsis skips; the manual-as-coach device is stronger on the page.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy takes action after hearing his troop is at risk of being dissolved. The Beagle Scouts set out to earn their fishing badges.
stories.perStorySynopsis: When Snoopy hears Beagle Scout headquarters is ready to dissolve his troop for never earning a single badge, the news sends him into a spiral. A copy of the official manual reframes the crisis: every challenge is a chance to shine, and a summer at camp is the chance to start earning. Snoopy packs his resolve along with the troop's sleeping bags , one step at a time.

stories.episodeTitle: A Beagle Scout Prepares / Teach a Bird to Fish
stories.situation: Marcie would rather stand on solid ground than set foot in a wobbly canoe, but a day of paddling and fishing is on the schedule.
stories.coping: Charlie Brown's patient coaching and a glassy lake win Marcie over. She discovers the calm of the water is its own reward and ends the day proud of herself for sticking with it.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis hands both badge halves to the Beagle Scouts; the script's second story is really a Marcie-and-Charlie Brown coaching story: Snoopy is present, but Marcie is who learns, and the patience-over-prize moral is explicit in the closing lines.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy takes action after hearing his troop is at risk of being dissolved. The Beagle Scouts set out to earn their fishing badges.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Snoopy turns up at Camp Spring Lake to earn his badges, and Charlie Brown signs on to coach the fishing half. The real journey belongs to Marcie, who distrusts wobbly canoes and steady water alike. Under Charlie Brown's gentle coaching she gives paddling a real try, finds the quiet of the lake is its own reward, and ends the day proud of the patience she did not know she had.

stories.situation: Naomi and Snoopy spend the day at ring toss, and Sally, who just called it a baby game, starts quietly panicking that being bad at things could cost her a best friend.
stories.coping: Secret practice with Charlie Brown, his reframe that a friend's talent is a chance to be proud of them, and Naomi's invitation to a game Sally can win at together.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis says Sally feels left out; the script shows the spiral underneath: the fear that a friend being good at things might expose what they don't share and end the friendship, plus the secret-training comedy. The friendship reframe is Charlie Brown's, not Sally's own discovery.
stories.synopsis: Sally feels left out when Naomi and Snoopy play ring toss. The kids write home about their best days at camp.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Naomi and Snoopy can't miss at ring toss, and Sally can't stand watching, because she'd already declared it a baby game, which makes sneaking off for secret training with Charlie Brown a little complicated. Her real fear isn't the score: if Naomi is great at things Sally isn't, what else might they not have in common? Charlie Brown's answer, friendship is how someone makes you feel, gets tested and holds, and the day ends over go fish with the whole crew.

stories.situation: Letter-writing day frames everyone's best camp stories, and Sally's is the one about being too scared for the creepy movie night.
stories.coping: A friend-built fear-tolerance plan, jump scares included, turns dread into delight, because being a little scared together is half the fun.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis's kids write home about their best days hides the structure: five letter-writers, one per kid, with Sally's scary-movie arc as the longest thread and Snoopy's memories-as-collection essay as the closing frame.
stories.synopsis: Sally feels left out when Naomi and Snoopy play ring toss. The kids write home about their best days at camp.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The campers sit down to write home, and every letter is a story: pranks swapped with Schroeder, a supermoon that beat expectations, a beagle troop learning that memories are the only collection worth keeping. Sally's letter takes the longest: she was dreading the camp's creepy-movie night, and a friend's jump-scare training course had to be built first. By the time she signs off, the scariest night of the summer has become one of its best, especially with everyone scared together.

stories.episodeTitle: Camp Crush / Counselor for a Day
stories.situation: Peppermint Patty decides Charlie Brown has a crush on her, mounts a full evidence-gathering operation, and braces to let him down gently at the barn dance.
stories.coping: Marcie's advice, kindness and honesty, gets the letdown over with: they are friends, they dance as friends, and Charlie Brown remains cheerfully oblivious.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: script shows the evidence scenes (a decoration invitation, a botched pep talk, a little too much closeness) misread one by one, and the tractor-repair B-plot paying off the dance; the joke is that Patty never verifies the crush.
stories.synopsis: Peppermint Patty is convinced Charlie Brown has a crush on her and wants to let him down easy. Marcie is chosen to be camp counselor for a day.
stories.perStorySynopsis: One friendly greeting from Charlie Brown, and Peppermint Patty has her verdict: he's got a crush, the barn dance will force the issue, and she'll have to break his heart kindly. The evidence mounts as the dance approaches, and at the big moment she delivers the letdown: they're friends, and they'll dance as friends. Charlie Brown's response confirms he never knew what she was talking about.

stories.episodeTitle: Camp Crush / Counselor for a Day
stories.situation: Marcie wins the counselor-for-a-day draw and fills the schedule with her idea of fun (yoga, tree-ring counting, life-sized chess) while the campers hope for s'mores.
stories.coping: Charlie Brown's nudge, plan a day you'd love, gets tested when the campers call the chess day boring, then get hooked once they wing the rules; Marcie's only real goal was everyone having fun.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). title-card variant: on-screen card reads Counsellor For a Day vs catalog Counselor for a Day. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis stops at Marcie is chosen; the script carries the actual arc: her anxiety about disappointing anyone, the dull morning, Charlie Brown's quiet advocacy, and the pawns-revolt ending that vindicates her.
stories.synopsis: Peppermint Patty is convinced Charlie Brown has a crush on her and wants to let him down easy. Marcie is chosen to be camp counselor for a day.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The counselor-for-a-day draw goes to Marcie, who stays up late squeezing everyone's dream activities into five-minute slots, until Charlie Brown talks her into planning a day she'd love instead. Yoga, stump-counting and life-sized chess hit the campers like a surprise quiz, and Marcie overhears enough to think she's ruined everything. But boredom has a way of becoming curiosity: the campers wing the chess rules, the pawns revolt on their own, and Marcie gets exactly what she wanted.

stories.episodeTitle: Sally's Tooth / The Chewing Gum Dilemma
stories.situation: Sally loses a tooth at camp and realizes the tooth fairy has no forwarding address for her, a logistics crisis with a quarter on the line.
stories.coping: Charlie Brown and Snoopy run an undercover tooth-fairy operation; a dog-biscuit mishap becomes a signed IOU, and Sally decides the tooth fairy's autograph beats cash anyway.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: script delivers the full caper: the letter with payment terms, Charlie Brown's only quarter, the decimal-point error that inflates the IOU, none of which the synopsis hints at. The wonder-preserving ending is the story, not the losing of the tooth.
stories.synopsis: Sally loses a tooth and worries the tooth fairy won't know she's at camp. Charlie Brown's fortunate find turns into candy chaos.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Sally's lost tooth is a windfall, since back teeth go for a quarter, until one flaw surfaces: the tooth fairy doesn't know she's at camp. A letter with payment terms goes out, and an undercover swap operation runs on Charlie Brown's last quarter and one beagle's steady paw. The dog biscuit under the pillow is an outrage, but the handwritten IOU, signed by the tooth fairy herself, turns the disaster into the best collectible in camp.

stories.episodeTitle: Sally's Tooth / The Chewing Gum Dilemma
stories.situation: Charlie Brown finds three pieces of gum at a gum-starved camp, and the whole camp's sudden niceness makes choosing two favorites an impossible popularity contest.
stories.coping: Cornered, he gives the gum away, keeping none and sharing none, on the logic that equal disappointment beats jealous friends, and the camp has to admit there are worse fates than a little more Charlie Brown.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis's fortunate find turns into candy chaos undersells the actual dilemma: flattery with a price tag, Sally's family-obligation claim, and the no-win fairness logic. The teamwork-manual interstitials mirror the gum standoff beat for beat.
stories.synopsis: Sally loses a tooth and worries the tooth fairy won't know she's at camp. Charlie Brown's fortunate find turns into candy chaos.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Charlie Brown finds a pack of gum with three pieces left, in a camp where the last piece got chewed days ago. Suddenly everyone's his friend: compliments flow, siblings cite family obligation, and the crowd demands he pick favorites. Cornered, he announces the gum is gone: all three pieces, thrown away, his included. Equal in their disappointment and equal in their outrage, the campers agree on something rare: the world could use a little more Charlie Brown.

stories.episodeTitle: Summer Friends / Last Day of Camp
stories.situation: Camp's last days are closing in, and Sally is avoiding her best friend rather than say goodbye, because she heard Naomi on the phone, excited to go home.
stories.coping: A paint run and a locked supply cabin force the two together, and the misunderstanding dissolves: Naomi was looking for her all day to promise friendship forever.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: the goodbye-to-a-friend situation plays for 2-4; the misunderstanding plot and irony land for 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis's Sally faces saying goodbye hides the avoidance plot (Sally dodges Naomi all day); the script's lock-in bonding montage (puzzles, sandcastles, music) carries the reconciliation, and the promise-to-stay-friends twist is Naomi's, not Sally's.
stories.synopsis: With camp nearing its end, Sally faces saying goodbye to her new friend Naomi. Snoopy and the Beagle Scouts race to earn one last badge.
stories.perStorySynopsis: With camp ending, Sally decides the kindest thing is to skip the goodbye entirely. She heard Naomi on the phone sounding thrilled to go home and assumes the friendship ends at the bus. Avoidance almost works, until a locked supply cabin strands them with jigsaw puzzles and time to talk. Naomi wasn't excited to leave; she'd been hunting Sally all day to make it official: friends forever.

stories.episodeTitle: Summer Friends / Last Day of Camp
stories.situation: On the last day, Charlie Brown tallies a summer of no ribbons and no awards, a memory wall he reads as a museum of things gone wrong, while Snoopy's troop comes up one badge short of staying a troop.
stories.coping: The campers recount what Charlie Brown actually gave them, confidence, encouragement, a friend who showed up, and the friendship badge saves Snoopy's troop while showing that winning is a moment and kindness lasts.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis splits into a badge race; the script braids the two threads, Charlie Brown's failure tally and Snoopy's missing badge, into one payoff: the friendship badge is both the last badge and Charlie Brown's award. Hopeless marks the season's darkest beat (Charlie Brown calls himself a failure); the resolution lands it.
stories.synopsis: With camp nearing its end, Sally faces saying goodbye to her new friend Naomi. Snoopy and the Beagle Scouts race to earn one last badge.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Last day of camp, and the accounting is grim: Charlie Brown's picture wall reads like a museum of things that went wrong, and Snoopy's troop is one badge short of official status. Then the campers take turns recounting what Charlie Brown actually did all summer, the encouragement, the rescued moments, the showing up, and the Beagle Scout manual declares friendship its highest honor. Snoopy's troop earns its last badge, Charlie Brown earns his first award, and both come from the same place.

stories.episodeTitle: Homesick Sally / Red Haired Letter Day
stories.situation: It is Sally's first summer at camp and she can't sleep, won't eat the oatmeal, and insists she is absolutely not homesick. The bed, obviously, is at fault.
stories.coping: Sally admits out loud that she might be a little homesick after caring for a lost baby bird, and a new friend shows her that not enjoying camp is better with someone else.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). vocabulary correction (2026-11-12): homesickness is ratified; emotion re-tagged from 'lonely, sad' to 'homesick, lonely'. mixed age: the homesickness situation plays for 2-4, the denial jokes and irony land for 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: script adds the denial armor (only little kids get homesick), the replica-bedroom bird subplot, and Naomi's shared-misery invitation that the synopsis compresses to a new friend hopping into her life.
stories.synopsis: Sally struggles to adjust to camp, but a new friend hops into her life. Charlie Brown enlists Snoopy's help to deliver a special letter.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Sally's first nights at camp are sleepless, and she'd rather blame lumpy oatmeal and lousy beds than admit she misses home. Then a strange little bird turns up in her bag, and building it a replica of her bedroom forces the truth into the open. When a fellow camper named Naomi suggests the things you don't enjoy are better not-enjoyed together, camp finally starts to feel survivable.

stories.episodeTitle: Homesick Sally / Red Haired Letter Day
stories.situation: Charlie Brown learns the Little Red-Haired Girl is at the camp across the lake and stakes everything on one letter, one cardboard-boat regatta, and a beagle courier.
stories.coping: When the letter delivery goes hilariously wrong, Charlie Brown still gets a scrap of reply (she knows part of his name), and he chooses to treat the almost as a win.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). title-card variant: on-screen card reads Red-Haired Letter Day (hyphenated) vs catalog Red Haired Letter Day. script_vs_synopsis: script shows the win-the-regatta-so-he-won't-have-to-speak strategy and the partial-reply payoff; the synopsis's courier summary undersells how wrong the delivery goes and how small-but-real the win is.
stories.synopsis: Sally struggles to adjust to camp, but a new friend hops into her life. Charlie Brown enlists Snoopy's help to deliver a special letter.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Charlie Brown finds out the Little Red-Haired Girl is closer than she's ever been, at the camp right across the lake, and drafts a letter inviting her to the cardboard boat regatta. Snoopy takes on courier duty, circles the entire lake, and returns with nothing but a page from Sally's activity book. Then a torn scrap of reply drifts in: she knows part of his name, and for Charlie Brown that's the best day of the summer.

stories.episodeTitle: To Dive or Not to Dive / Foul Weather Friends
stories.segmentTitle: To Dive or Not to Dive
stories.situation: A belly-flop from last summer, and the nickname that came with it, has Peppermint Patty refusing to dive, even with Snoopy coaching her at the dock.
stories.coping: Sharing fears with friends normalizes hers, because everyone is afraid of something, and Patty finally takes the plunge, then finds her lost duck floatie waiting in the splash.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: script names the belly-flop backstory and the nickname that keeps the fear alive; synopsis-only tagging would read this as plain fear of water, but the fear is shame-driven, which changes the emotion tag.
stories.synopsis: Peppermint Patty's fear of diving sends her Snoopy's way. The Beagle Scouts attempt to build a shelter as Sally and Naomi fight over bracelets.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Peppermint Patty will cannonball, float and splash, but she will not dive, not since last summer's belly flop earned her a nickname she never shook. When Snoopy's coaching stalls at the edge of the platform, the campers trade their own silly fears to show her she's in good company. Patty finally takes the plunge, and the whole dock cheers.

stories.episodeTitle: To Dive or Not to Dive / Foul Weather Friends
stories.situation: A rainy-day craft session turns Sally and Naomi's friendship-bracelet styles into a standoff, with Linus drafted as the unwilling go-between.
stories.coping: A well-timed reminder that there is no right or wrong way to make something for a friend lands, the girls trade honest compliments and bracelets, and the friendship survives the glitter.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis's fight over bracelets becomes, on the page, a conflict between two philosophies of friendship, tight and steadfast versus flexible and colorful, with Linus's scissor-relay comedy in the middle.
stories.synopsis: Peppermint Patty's fear of diving sends her Snoopy's way. The Beagle Scouts attempt to build a shelter as Sally and Naomi fight over bracelets.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Rain traps the campers indoors, and Sally and Naomi decide friendship bracelets will cure the blahs, until each decides the other is doing it wrong. Knots, beads and glitter become a proxy war, with Linus relaying messages between two friends who are absolutely not speaking. When the bickering finally meets a reminder that there's no right or wrong way to make something for a friend, the girls trade bracelets, and the friendship comes out tighter than ever.

stories.situation: Snoopy's troop tackles the foraging badge while a flock of lookalike birds keeps making off with the camp's food, and keeping cool becomes the real skill.
stories.coping: Assess the situation, adapt, try again, then ask for help: the manual's ladder keeps the troop level-headed, and a patient forager finds that nature provides one way or another.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script runs a double foraging story: the Beagle Scouts' berry-picking badge and Peppermint Patty and Marcie's vanishing picnic, which the synopsis flattens into a single mission.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy and the Beagle Scouts embark on a mission to earn their foraging badges. Charlie Brown is determined to win a "Piney" award.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Foraging badge day means one thing to Snoopy's troop: blueberries. The manual walks them through finding, picking and staying calm when the food supply keeps disappearing, because a flock of blueberry-colored birds has plans of its own, and the campers' picnic is not safe either. Step by calm step, the troop learns that when every fix fails, the last move is asking for help, and that a patient forager never really goes hungry.

stories.situation: Charlie Brown has never won a Piney award, and day after day of near-misses (politeness, jokes, even dignity) starts to wear him down.
stories.coping: He swings for the fences one more time, getting the camp banner out of a tall tree; Snoopy wins the Piney, but Charlie Brown accepts a special certificate for trying the most, and decides that counts.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: script supplies the full losing streak (toast, tidiest bunk to Pigpen, politeness, knock-knock) and the lost-the-most certificate beat that gives the story its ending; the synopsis's determination is the setup only.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy and the Beagle Scouts embark on a mission to earn their foraging badges. Charlie Brown is determined to win a "Piney" award.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The daily Piney awards keep going to everyone but Charlie Brown. Even Pigpen wins tidiest bunk. He tries politeness, comedy and finally a grand gesture: retrieving Spring Lake's legendary banner from the top of a tall tree. The Piney goes to Snoopy, but the camp hands Charlie Brown a certificate honoring his many, many attempts, and for once, almost is enough.

stories.episodeTitle: Campfire Yarns / Beagle Point or Bust
stories.situation: It is spooky-story night around the campfire, and Charlie Brown's tale is the only one that doesn't scare anybody.
stories.coping: His story of a day when everything went wrong, true events as it happens, lands as the scariest of the night, and a suspiciously animated shrub shows up to prove it.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis says Charlie Brown is lost for words; the script shows his real problem, stories that keep coming out as his own bad days, and gives him a payoff the synopsis never mentions.
stories.synopsis: The kids tell scary campfire stories, but Charlie Brown is lost for words. Snoopy's journal sheds light on an ill-fated canoe voyage to Beagle Point.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The campers trade spooky stories by the fire: a haunted tire-pressure warning, a boy whose hands play only rock and roll, a girl cursed to eat pizza forever. Charlie Brown's turn is a dud, and everyone knows it. But when he tells the tale of a day when absolutely everything went wrong, the campfire gets its chills the honest way: every word is true, and the haunted shrub is closer than anyone thinks.

stories.episodeTitle: Campfire Yarns / Beagle Point or Bust
stories.situation: Snoopy's mailed-home journal retells the troop's canoe voyage to Beagle Point, a voyage his own narration keeps insisting was somebody else's fault.
stories.coping: The journal's last pages drop the spin: a good leader, and a good friend, has to know when to listen, and the sunset at Beagle Point is best shared with the troop that mutinied.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis calls it an ill-fated canoe voyage, full stop; the script frames it as an unreliable narrator's confession: the solo decisions, the portage fiasco, the mutiny, which is where the listening lesson lives.
stories.synopsis: The kids tell scary campfire stories, but Charlie Brown is lost for words. Snoopy's journal sheds light on an ill-fated canoe voyage to Beagle Point.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Mail call brings Charlie Brown a used book from his dog: Snoopy's swashbuckling account of the troop's canoe expedition to Beagle Point. As the campers gather to listen, the great leader's version of events takes credit for every high and blames the mutiny on everyone else, until the journal itself admits the truth. A good leader has to know when to listen, and the sunset at Beagle Point is lovelier with the whole troop there.

A good leader has to know when to listen, and the sunset at Beagle Point is lovelier with the whole troop there.

stories.situation: A single mosquito appoints itself Snoopy's nemesis, and ignoring it, the camp's best advice, turns out to be easier said than done.
stories.coping: No strategy works, not ignoring it and not a pillow-fight distraction, and the standoff ends with beagle and bug bunking under the stars; some opponents you just learn to outlast.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). title-card variant: on-screen card reads Beagle Versus Bug vs catalog Beagle vs Bug. script_vs_synopsis: script adds a Sally bed-monster crossover (the monster under her bunk is Snoopy fleeing the mosquito), which the synopsis omits entirely.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy encounters a new nemesis: a mosquito that won't leave him alone. Schroeder thinks the camp's official song is due for an update.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Snoopy arrives at camp with a nemesis: one mosquito that follows him everywhere, humming just out of reach. Charlie Brown prescribes the classics (ignore it, put it out of your mind), but the bug proves immune to patience. By lights-out the feud has chased Snoopy under Sally's bunk, and when the campers discover the monster in their room, beagle and mosquito both end up under the stars.

stories.situation: Schroeder can't stand the camp's catchy-but-endless rally song, so he quietly invents a songwriting contest to replace it.
stories.coping: A night of new entries, including his own Beethoven-flavored act, teaches Schroeder what he'd forgotten: the old song is fun and full of joy, and the original stays.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: script shows Schroeder's contest is a fabrication and stages his confession-and-reversal ending (the old song stays), which the synopsis's due-for-an-update framing never hints at.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy encounters a new nemesis: a mosquito that won't leave him alone. Schroeder thinks the camp's official song is due for an update.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The official Spring Lake rally song greets every morning, every meal and every activity, and Schroeder has finally had enough. He invents a camp song contest with the promise of immortality for the winner, and the campers deliver, and even Schroeder takes the stage with a Beethoven twist. But somewhere between the entries and the sing-alongs he rediscovers what made the old song work: it is fun, it is full of joy, and it is exactly what camp sounds like. The original stays.

stories.episodeTitle: Leave It Like You Found It / Camp Mascot
stories.segmentTitle: Leave It Like You Found It
stories.situation: An orienteering hike leads the kids to a picture-perfect hidden spot, and their playtime trashes it, until Linus refuses to let it slide.
stories.coping: Charlie Brown reframes the mess, the spot was never theirs, and the kids clean it up until it looks like they were never there, leaving prouder than they arrived.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). vocabulary correction (2026-11-12): guilt is ratified; the pivot feeling is now tagged guilty, with calm kept for the nature-appreciation frame. script_vs_synopsis: script gives Linus the conscience role and the leave-no-trace framing; the synopsis's playtime upsets Linus undersells that the kids come around and do the work.
stories.synopsis: The Beagle Scouts and the kids enjoy a hidden oasis, but their playtime upsets Linus. Charlie Brown and Snoopy compete to be camp mascot.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Charlie Brown's orienteering prize is a hidden clearing too beautiful to disturb, so the kids don't let that stop them. Snacks, sketches and games pile up until Linus has had enough: the spot isn't theirs, and they owe it to everyone else to leave it as they found it. One cleanup montage later the clearing looks untouched, and the kids head home a little prouder than they arrived.

stories.episodeTitle: Leave It Like You Found It / Camp Mascot
stories.situation: Charlie Brown feels camp passing him by, so a mascot contest against his own dog looks like the new experience he's been missing.
stories.coping: Snoopy wins the crowd and then resigns on the spot; Charlie Brown turns the job down too, because if he's broadening his horizons he'd rather do it as himself.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: synopsis frames this as a competition for camp mascot; the script's actual arc is Charlie Brown learning the new experience he wanted was being himself, and the resignation twist is entirely missing from the synopsis.
stories.synopsis: The Beagle Scouts and the kids enjoy a hidden oasis, but their playtime upsets Linus. Charlie Brown and Snoopy compete to be camp mascot.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Charlie Brown can feel camp happening to everyone but him, so when the mascot sign-up sheet promises new experiences and broader horizons, he takes the bait. The contest is a boy against his dog, and the dog, relying on personality alone, wins going away. Then Snoopy slides the camp a resignation letter, the job lands on Charlie Brown, and he surprises everyone by declining: if he's going to grow, he'd rather do it as himself.

stories.situation: Linus' beloved blanket unravels on a hike and disappears, and suddenly the camp's most self-possessed camper can't sit still or say why, though everyone knows why.
stories.coping: Charlie Brown names what no one else will, that comfort isn't a crutch, and Lucy quietly barters a can of nickels to bring the blanket home.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: the comfort-object situation plays for 2-4; the sibling comedy and Socrates asides land for 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: synopsis says frazzled; the script gives the loss real weight: Lucy's mockery, Charlie Brown's defense of comfort objects, and Lucy's nickel barter make a tender arc, not a gag, which is where the provisional vibe (calm, not silly) comes from.
stories.synopsis: Linus' blanket gets snagged and unravels on a hike, leaving him frazzled. Snoopy tries to crash the kids' build-your-own-pizza night.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Linus' blanket catches on a branch during capture the flag, and by lunchtime there's almost nothing left of it. Lucy prescribes tough love, Charlie Brown admits the camp feels sadder with Linus so sad, and Linus tries, really tries, to be one-eighth of himself. Then the blanket reappears, traded home by a sister who'd never say it out loud.

stories.situation: Snoopy is barred from make-your-own-pizza night, registered campers only, and has to watch the whole camp eat without him.
stories.coping: Charlie Brown keeps ending up with more pizza than he can eat, and when the gate finally opens the lesson lands: the best pizza is the one you share.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: the exclusion-and-sharing situation plays for 2-4; the topping jokes and rulebook satire land for 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: script adds Charlie Brown's quiet generosity and his own topping-choice paralysis gag; the synopsis's tries to crash misses that the sharing starts before the door ever opens.
stories.synopsis: Linus' blanket gets snagged and unravels on a hike, leaving him frazzled. Snoopy tries to crash the kids' build-your-own-pizza night.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Make-your-own-pizza night has one rule: registered campers only. Snoopy lobbies, lurks and gets the gate anyway, but the night keeps tilting his way: the topping table mysteriously shrinks, and Charlie Brown somehow has more pizza than any one boy can eat. By the time the beagle is finally let in, the camp's rulebook has met its better idea, and everyone learns the only thing better than making your own pizza is sharing your own pizza.

stories.episodeTitle: Bed Heads & Beagle Care / The Great Gold Rush
stories.situation: A case of camp hair so severe it stops Charlie Brown leaving the cabin, while Snoopy's troop grooms, feeds and bathes him for the Beagle Care badge.
stories.coping: Snoopy peeks out from under his own worst hair day, the two share a laugh, and Charlie Brown chooses the remaining days of camp over hiding.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). title-card variant: on-screen card reads Bed Heads and Beagle Care vs catalog Bed Heads & Beagle Care. script_vs_synopsis: synopsis leads with the dog-care badge; the script's emotional core is Charlie Brown's hiding-out arc and Snoopy's hat-hair solidarity. The badge is the setup, and the rejoining-the-day is the story.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy wants the Beagle Scouts to try for the dog-care badge, by pampering him. A scavenger hunt sends the kids on a wild goose chase.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Charlie Brown wakes to a full-blown case of camp hair, and no brush, blow-dryer or wig from the costume trunk can tame it, so he decides to stop attending camp until it does. Snoopy, hiding from the same problem with worse hair, shows him there is only one cure: laughing at it. Charlie Brown trades the rec cabin for the sunshine and the days he would have missed.

stories.episodeTitle: Bed Heads & Beagle Care / The Great Gold Rush
stories.situation: The annual gold-rush scavenger hunt turns camp competitive: Peppermint Patty's foolproof system versus Marcie's Klondike homework versus Linus just wanting the chocolate-coin version.
stories.coping: The system fails, the bookworm wins by accident, and the hunters who struck out decide a ribbon shared beats gold hoarded, then wish it were an Easter egg hunt again.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis's wild goose chase reads as aimless comedy; the script runs it as a gold-fever satire in which the narration describes neighbors turning on each other. The competitive-meanness beat is real, and the shared-ribbon ending is the lesson. synopsis column repunctuated to meet the house dash rule; the catalog Episodes sheet keeps the original text.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy wants the Beagle Scouts to try for the dog-care badge, by pampering him. A scavenger hunt sends the kids on a wild goose chase.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Gold rush day: the counselors hide gold-painted rocks, and Peppermint Patty has a foolproof system built on years of watching where the gold gets hidden. The system fails, the hiding spots have moved, and gold fever sets the campers against each other while Marcie, who stayed behind with a book on the actual Klondike, wanders off with the win. Nobody keeps the gold, everyone splits the ribbon, and Linus files his verdict: worst Easter egg hunt ever.

stories.episodeTitle: Following in the Pawprints / Roughing It
stories.situation: The Beagle Scouts have lost their camp enthusiasm, and Snoopy turns to the handbook's tales of the First Beagle Scout to find the inspiration that will get his troop moving.
stories.coping: reframing/distraction
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script runs a double inspiration story, Snoopy hunting the handbook for motivation while Charlie Brown hunts an early-summer fish, and lands the real lesson in Snoopy's realization that the First Beagle Scout's secret was the great outdoors itself, a turn the synopsis never makes.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy looks to the famous First Beagle Scout to help motivate his lazy troop. Feeling like camp is too easy, Peppermint Patty tries roughing it.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Back at camp for another summer, Snoopy finds his troop has gone stone-cold lazy, and inspiration is nowhere in the tent. The handbook sends him hunting the legend of the First Beagle Scout, whose determination crossed any river and tamed nature with a look. Reading the stories aloud gets him nowhere, until he sees it: the point was never what the First Beagle Scout did, it was what inspired him. The great outdoors. One hike later, the troop is moving again, and the summer is officially on.

stories.episodeTitle: Following in the Pawprints / Roughing It
stories.situation: Camp feels too easy to Peppermint Patty, all candle workshops and cushy mattresses, so she sets out to rough it the way she believes her dad's generation did.
stories.coping: reframing/distraction
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script builds the arc on Patty's letter home, which lands the ending in her own words, going overboard taught her the value of comfort, good friends and a delicious meal, plus the guess that her dad planned it that way all along. emotion silly appears on the ratified list; the felt tone here is comedy throughout, tagged against the guide's 21 terms.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy looks to the famous First Beagle Scout to help motivate his lazy troop. Feeling like camp is too easy, Peppermint Patty tries roughing it.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Convinced camp has gone soft, Peppermint Patty recruits Snoopy for a week of the way camp used to be: leaf beds, rainwater off a leaf, cold beans straight from the can, and a toothbrush twig. She loves it, loudly, right up until the smell of her friends' sloppy joes drifts across the lake. One quick visit for a hello becomes dinner, and her letter home confesses the truth: roughing it taught her exactly what comfort, company and a good meal are worth, and she suspects that was her dad's plan all along.

stories.episodeTitle: Junior Counselor / Too Cool for Camp
stories.situation: Charlie Brown is made Official Junior Counselor, longest-attending camper in camp history, and tries so hard to run the perfect camp that he takes the fun out of it.
stories.coping: apologizing
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). synopsis punctuation: catalog text uses an em dash after junior counselor, repunctuated here for the house dash rule; the catalog Episodes sheet keeps the original. script_vs_synopsis: the script adds the stakes (his one chance at respect), the verdict (worst Junior Counselor ever, technically the first), the popcorn apology, and the resignation that lands as a relief.
stories.synopsis: Charlie Brown becomes a junior counselor and the camp stickler. Joe Cool makes an appearance at summer camp, but it isn't his scene.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Summons to the Head Counselor's office, dish duty presumed, and instead Charlie Brown learns he is the longest-attending camper in camp history and the first-ever Official Junior Counselor. He appoints Snoopy associate (no hurt feelings), then sets about perfecting everyone's fun: umbrella angles, water safety, marshmallow stick calibration. The campers' review is unanimous, the worst Junior Counselor ever. His apology is popcorn, popped en masse, his resignation letter follows, and with the whistle gone the fun comes back, along with the discovery that trying less can be the trying-hardest thing of all.

stories.episodeTitle: Junior Counselor / Too Cool for Camp
stories.situation: Joe Cool arrives at Camp Spring Lake, too cool to fetch, too cool to hold a kite, and too cool to be the Beagle Scout leader his campers actually need.
stories.coping: trying again
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script's turning point is an object, not a lecture: Linus leaves Joe Cool's Beagle Scout gear by the lost and found, with a word about the world-famous leader the camp used to have, and the transformation happens off-page; the synopsis's isn't-his-scene framing undersells the cost, that cool isolated him from the job he loves.
stories.synopsis: Charlie Brown becomes a junior counselor and the camp stickler. Joe Cool makes an appearance at summer camp, but it isn't his scene.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Camp Spring Lake gets a new camper: Joe Cool, dark black shades, cold ice water in the veins, too cool to teeter or totter. Also too cool to fetch, hold a kite, move for lunch, or do any of the helpful, adventuring, nature-exploring things a certain world-famous Beagle Scout leader used to do. His campers miss their leader, and Linus makes the case without a single word: the scout gear, left by the lost and found, no longer useful to anyone too cool to need it. Somewhere between the shades and the whistle, the world-famous Beagle Scout Leader comes back, and wonders briefly if the sunglasses might still look cool. Good grief.

stories.episodeTitle: The Marshmallow Tree / The Balancing Rock
stories.situation: A missing-bird poster goes up and the campers turn junior detectives, tracking the case to a lost hanky that means everything to its owner.
stories.coping: asking for help
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). synopsis mismatch flagged: the catalog text reads a scout disappears; the script's case is a missing pet bird and the recovery of Suzie Snoozy's hanky, no missing scout; tagged on the script. the closing moral, it's the little things you don't appreciate until they're gone, is the script's, not the synopsis's.
stories.synopsis: When a scout disappears, Snoopy and the troop leave no stone unturned. The Beagle Scouts take on more than they can carry while trying to help.
stories.perStorySynopsis: A hand-drawn poster of a missing bird goes up, and Camp Spring Lake opens a full investigation: tire-swing witnesses, branch-by-branch sweeps, Franklin's aerodynamic theories mercifully beside the point. The trail leads somewhere unexpected, to a hanky belonging to Suzie Snoozy, off duty with a cold and not the same without it, and one pillow-feather-flecked pillow fort later, the case closes with the treasure found. The campers hand it over a little wistful themselves, because everyone learned the same thing on this case: it's the little things you don't appreciate until they're gone.

stories.episodeTitle: The Marshmallow Tree / The Balancing Rock
stories.situation: On the one free day with no sign-ups and no schedule, Peppermint Patty plans the hike of the summer to the Balancing Rock, and Marcie brings her library.
stories.coping: patience
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script gives the day its texture, Snoopy hauling Marcie's encyclopedias, Patty's field guide in action (pointy tree, leafy tree, other leafy tree, carpet tree, which is moss), and the Wordsworth line that lands the day: nature never did betray the heart that loved her.
stories.synopsis: When a scout disappears, Snoopy and the troop leave no stone unturned. The Beagle Scouts take on more than they can carry while trying to help.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Free day, no activities, one plan: Peppermint Patty and Snoopy are hiking to the Balancing Rock, a big rock perfectly balanced on a big rock, and how it got there nobody knows. Marcie comes too, bringing a little reading, which turns out to be enough books to stock a cabin, and Beagle Scout helping-hands protocol absorbs the cargo. On the trail, Patty invents her own field guides (pointy tree, carpet tree) while Marcie translates (fir, linden, maple, moss), and at the summit, rock and rock and one well-earned view, the day's poet laureate finds the perfect reading spot. Wordsworth, natural light, wonderful company, and one beagle who came through.

stories.situation: Charlie Brown hands every decision of his summer to Snoopy's paper fortune teller, right up until the boot-buster trail needs a choice and the fortune teller is gone.
stories.coping: trying again
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). synopsis mismatch flagged: the catalog pairs this story with Woodstock's toy obsession, which belongs to a different episode; the script's second story is the Perseid meteor shower, tagged on the script and noted for catalog review. script_vs_synopsis: the script lands the actual arc, fortune teller lost on the summit, moss on the north side, anthills to the south, and Charlie Brown navigating himself home, with the open question of whether Snoopy lost the contraption on purpose.
stories.synopsis: Indecisive Charlie Brown decides to leave his fate to a paper fortune teller. Woodstock's new toy soon becomes a full-blown obsession.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Choosing between tennis and kayaking has Charlie Brown paralyzed, so Snoopy's paper fortune teller takes over: bait or cheese, jelly or vanilla, fastball or curve. Life is finally decision-free, right up until the boot-buster trail, camp's hardest hike, ends at a fork after dark and the fortune teller is nowhere in the pack. Panic, then moss on the north side of a tree, then an anthill facing the sun, then east, the direction of camp. Charlie Brown walks himself home, and when Linus asks if the fortune teller worked, the answer is better: they lost it, and this was all him. Whether a certain beagle engineered the whole lesson, Charlie Brown chooses to believe.

stories.perStorySynopsis: The Perseid meteor shower is a one-night-a-year event (a month of nights, per Marcie), and the camp telescope is buried somewhere in the supply shed, which may have been the counselors' plan all along. The meteors arrive on schedule, fireballs over a dark lake, and a camper who drove the whole camp to this moment admits to feeling a little small, then, in the same breath, pretty special to have been here for it.

stories.situation: Sally is upset, and Detective Snoopy and Charlie Brown work the whole camp for leads on what happened, pancake breakfast through fairy houses through kazoo, with no answer that adds up.
stories.coping: naming the feeling
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script's mystery is a mismatch case, every witness reports a perfect day, and the reveal inverts the genre: the tears are happy tears over a perfect day, and the sadness inside them is just the knowledge that perfect days don't happen all the time; Charlie Brown's closing, that perfect days can happen anytime and it's up to us to notice, is the moral and missing from the synopsis.
stories.synopsis: Detective Snoopy and Charlie Brown must figure out why Sally's upset. It's time to fill up the camp memory book, and Lucy wants it to be perfect.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Sally is crying, claims she's fine, and the case is open: Detective Snoopy and associate Charlie Brown work the camp for what went wrong. Every lead comes back impossible: pancakes the whole cabin agreed were the best of the summer, fairy houses that turned out great, a kazoo turn, a swim, ice cream, a nature walk. By all accounts, Sally had a wonderful day. The confession explains everything: she feels so lucky and happy that her feelings don't know what to do with themselves, and it comes out her eyes. Happy tears, with a little sadness folded in, because perfect days end. Her big brother's closing note to the case: perfect days can happen anytime, and noticing them is the job.

stories.situation: Lucy is in charge of the camp memory book, the yearbook of the summer, and decides that if the campers' memories aren't photogenic enough, she'll stage better ones.
stories.coping: reframing/distraction
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script runs the perfectionism to its failure and past it: mashed-potato ice cream, a bear suit that isn't a bear suit, memories nobody remembers making, and the campers laughing at the book anyway; Charlie Brown's rescue line, they're laughing at the memories they made having fun with their friends, turns Lucy's flop into the best memory book camp ever had.
stories.synopsis: Detective Snoopy and Charlie Brown must figure out why Sally's upset. It's time to fill up the camp memory book, and Lucy wants it to be perfect.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Camp ends in two days, the memory book is Lucy's to build, and camp's legacy is on the line. The campers' actual memories let her down: rereading Moby Dick, walks in the woods, sitting on steps telling stories. Boring. So she stages better ones: less splishy-splashy, more enthusiasm, cold mashed potatoes standing in for ice cream, a bear chase with whatever that costume is. The great reveal lands with the campers laughing at her, until Charlie Brown names what's actually happening: they're laughing at the memories they made with their friends, which is what camp is all about. By the last page the book is signed by everyone, and even Lucy, handed a good dog and a compliment she can't refute, believes it.

stories.episodeTitle: Big Fish Called Big Red / Listen Up, Kid
stories.situation: Rain cancels practice and traps the campers indoors, so bunk-story time turns into three competing versions of the legend of Big Red, the giant catfish of Camp Spring Lake.
stories.coping: naming the feeling
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script's engine is the three-version structure (Sally's swashbuckler, Lucy's blame-the-assistant tale, Charlie Brown's everyone-together ending) and the punchline that the fish probably never existed, just a mischievous beagle; the synopsis's rain-and-stories setup misses that the last storyteller wins by making the legend a group effort.
stories.synopsis: A rainy day sets the scene for stories about legendary fish Big Red. The gang tries to cheer up an unhappy camper.
stories.perStorySynopsis: A rain-soaked afternoon calls for bunk stories, and the legend of Big Red gets three tellings. In Sally's version only the world-famous fisher beagle can catch the boat-bumping, toe-tickling catfish. Lucy's recast puts a brilliant, perfect fisherwoman in charge and pins the ruined legacy on her good-for-nothing beagle assistant. Charlie Brown's version hands the job to everyone, who get so busy enjoying a beautiful day together they forget the fish entirely. Sally's verdict question goes unanswered by her big brother, who suspects the only monster in the lake was a prank-loving beagle all along.

stories.situation: Shirley, a first-year camper, is having a bad day in plain sight, and the whole camp takes turns trying to joke, cheer and hustle her into having fun.
stories.coping: asking for comfort
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis's unhappy camper hides the actual mechanics: every fix fails (pep talk, aardvark joke, forced fetch), Marcie supplies the listening idea, and Snoopy's silent company is what opens Shirley up, with her own admission that she is new, shy, and just wants someone to listen.
stories.synopsis: A rainy day sets the scene for stories about legendary fish Big Red. The gang tries to cheer up an unhappy camper.
stories.perStorySynopsis: First-year camper Shirley is not having fun, and Camp Spring Lake deploys its full arsenal: Lucy's activity lectures, Snoopy's A-material knock-knock joke, a beagle-supervised cheer-up campaign. Nothing lands. Then Snoopy simply sits beside her, and Shirley finally says what she needed all along: camp is great, she just doesn't know anyone, and she wants someone to listen. The campers own the miss, and listening to each other turns a bad day into a sandcastle afternoon.

stories.coping: apologizing
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script supplies the delegation disaster (Snoopy sorts by birth month, delivers balloons early, opens everything) plus the Lucy beat, that the job was her idea, and the arc lands on Charlie Brown taking the blame, relieving his associate of duty, and finishing the route together.
stories.synopsis: Charlie Brown realizes being the camp postmaster is no easy task. Naomi gets Snoopy hooked on the art of crafting.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Camp postmaster sounds like a hero's job until Charlie Brown sees the parcel pile, so he deputizes Snoopy to help. The beagle's delivery protocol (sort by birth month, taste-test the cookies, release the birthday balloons) turns the route into a catastrophe, and Lucy's verdict is swift: what kind of blockhead lets his dog deliver the mail? Charlie Brown owns it, relieves his associate of duty, then wins him back for the birthday balloon rescue and the rest of the deliveries. The route gets done the hard way, together, with an apology in the middle.

stories.coping: reframing/distraction
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script carries the escalation (pencil holders, a macaroni basketball net to regulation height, a papier-mache shirt) and Naomi's recovery line, that crafting is about imagination, so let the world be your crafting closet, which Snoopy takes a little too literally; the closing observation that getting carried away always ends someplace new is the moral and is missing from the synopsis.
stories.synopsis: Charlie Brown realizes being the camp postmaster is no easy task. Naomi gets Snoopy hooked on the art of crafting.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Naomi shows Snoopy the joy of crafting, and the beagle turns out to have a gift. Ice-pop-stick boats become a working wharf district, then a pencil holder, a shade canopy, and a macaroni basketball net at regulation height, until the camp's supplies are gone and the supply closet is closed. Naomi's fix is a philosophy: crafting was never about supplies, it's about imagination. Which Snoopy hears as permission to de-stick every ice pop in camp and rebuild his masterpiece from the parts. The camp gets its things back, and the beagle gets a new way of seeing everything.

stories.coping: trying again

stories.synopsis: When Snoopy spends a day on shore, he takes up extreme sandcastle building. Peppermint Patty is determined to break a camp record.
stories.perStorySynopsis: A stylish nurse's bow and a dry-bandage order sideline Snoopy exactly as the camp's new floating playground arrives, and the beach ball is small comfort. Then Linus unveils Castle van Pelt, all parapets and guard towers, and the beagle's competitive engineering kicks in. Moats, walls and a central keep rise side by side, not that it's a competition, until the whole camp abandons the crowded water to build. By the time the bandage comes off, the playground looks a lot less crowded, and the beach has a skyline.

stories.synopsis: When Snoopy spends a day on shore, he takes up extreme sandcastle building. Peppermint Patty is determined to break a camp record.

Patty takes the reframe, and claims the one record that matters, best best friend, which she and Marcie agree to share.

stories.situation: Charlie Brown finds a perfect little clubhouse full of old baseball cards and spends the day agonizing over whether to keep it secret or share it.
stories.coping: talking it out
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script gives the secret its own comedy (the Joe Shlabotnik rookie card, the pine-cone cover story, a midnight conscience consult with Linus) and the twist ending, that everyone already knew about the clubhouse and thought it was a dump, leaving Charlie Brown and Snoopy with the treasure to themselves.
stories.synopsis: The discovery of a new clubhouse is a very hard secret to keep. Snoopy settles the great camp debate: hamburgers or hot dogs?
stories.perStorySynopsis: A walk to nowhere leads Charlie Brown to a little clubhouse stuffed with old baseball cards, Joe Shlabotnik memorabilia included, and for one perfect afternoon it is entirely his. Then the guilt moves in: everyone has a right to know, but with his luck, sharing means waiting outside. He tries a pine-cone cover story on Sally, wakes Linus for a midnight ruling, and finally confesses to the whole camp. The punchline is instant: they all knew about the clubhouse, always have, and who wants a cramped hut full of old cards? Which suits Charlie Brown and Snoopy just fine.

stories.situation: Camper's-choice dinner splits Camp Spring Lake into hot dog people and hamburger people, and the tiebreaker lands on the camp's only neutral party: Snoopy.
stories.coping: reframing/distraction
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script escalates the split into territory (hot dog craft cabin, hamburger hiking songs) and gives Snoopy a whole day of dodge-the-decision before the pizza reveal, a third option nobody put on the ballot, which is the actual resolution and absent from the synopsis.
stories.synopsis: The discovery of a new clubhouse is a very hard secret to keep. Snoopy settles the great camp debate: hamburgers or hot dogs?
stories.perStorySynopsis: Camper's-choice dinner night asks one question, and Camp Spring Lake splits down the middle: hot dogs, the official food of summer camp, versus hamburgers, delicious and dignified. The vote ties, the beagle tiebreaker becomes a full-time job, and by afternoon friends are pitted against friends, with the craft cabin hot-dog-only and the hiking trails patrolled by burger loyalists. Snoopy spends the day canoodling, canoeing and stacking firewood, all hamburger propaganda, until dinnertime forces his decision. The ruling comes out of the steamer: pizza. Nobody suggested pizza. Everybody eats.

stories.coping: asking for help
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script frames the story through Spike's letter and the interstitial on persistence, then runs the comedy of origin (why would a dog take cacti for a walk? the mysteries of nature), which the synopsis's impress-his-brother setup compresses; the resolution is a gift sent, not a lesson spoken.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy wants to impress his brother, but his troop is in poor form. After a prank, Sally wants Charlie Brown and Snoopy to get even on her behalf.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Mail call brings Snoopy a letter from his brother Spike in Needles, who has been so inspired by the tales of Camp Spring Lake that he is starting a Beagle Scout troop of his own. On the next hike, the troop stumbles on a botanical mystery: potted cacti, in the middle of the forest, and nobody's telling. While Lucy presses them into a Landscapes of America diorama and Marcie catalogs the species, Snoopy has his own plan. By day's end the cacti are walking out of the woods, destination Needles, a starter kit for the newest Beagle Scout troop in the desert.

stories.coping: standing up for yourself
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script runs the escalation both ways: Charlie Brown's polite talking-to works, Sally's counter-prank operation flops (free popcorn refused, dollar bill repossessed with a thank-you note), and the ending lands on Sally herself talking Charlie Brown out of a prank war; the synopsis's get-even framing stops at the setup.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy wants to impress his brother, but his troop is in poor form. After a prank, Sally wants Charlie Brown and Snoopy to get even on her behalf.
stories.perStorySynopsis: A sheet at the window, a cabin of screaming campers, and Sally is sure she saw a ghost, until the truth comes out: it was a prank by the big kids. Outrage replaces fear, and she drafts her big brother for revenge on grounds of family honor. Charlie Brown takes the high road and, remarkably, it works, the pranksters apologize. Sally is unmollified and launches her own operation with Snoopy, which the pranksters out-prank with a repossessed dollar bill. In the end it's Sally who calls it: no prank wars, the whole thing behind them, and a little sister quietly proud of her own good advice.

stories.coping: trying again
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis's broken-promise framing reads heavier than the script plays it: Snoopy is invited, hesitates, and the rodeo wins him over (hat, saddle, yeehaw), with no on-page guilt beat; the resolution is the troop cheering his lasso-contest trophy and the square dance, flagged here rather than forced into a guilt arc the text doesn't show.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy breaks a promise to his troop when he ditches them for a camp rodeo. Linus commits to proving the existence of a legendary critter.
stories.perStorySynopsis: It's rodeo day at Camp Spring Lake, lasso contest, wagon races, Pigpen's chili, and Lucy's self-elected sheriff's badge, and Snoopy is a natural with a rope before anyone hands him a hat. The call of the wild bucking bronco (a saddle on a log) proves irresistible, and the beagle rides off to compete. The lasso contest ends with the only contestant who actually roped a target taking the trophy, the square dance spins until everyone's dizzy, and the troop that came to watch does the cheering. A leader's day off, it turns out, is best spent where his troop can applaud.

stories.situation: Linus is determined to prove the Hedge Toad, a critter that disguises itself as rocks, shrubs and driftwood, is real, even with his sister and half the camp calling it hooey.
stories.coping: trying again
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). script_vs_synopsis: the script's engine is the debunking operation (Lucy and Charlie Brown hunting proof of nothing) colliding with Charlie Brown's defense of Linus's wonder, and Lucy's own reversal, there are no quitters in my family, which turns the blurry photo from failure into fuel; none of that is in the synopsis.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy breaks a promise to his troop when he ditches them for a camp rodeo. Linus commits to proving the existence of a legendary critter.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Linus is on the trail of the Hedge Toad, the most nefarious animal in the forest, notorious for disguising itself as rocks, shrubs and driftwood before it pounces. Lucy mounts a debunking expedition with Snoopy, determined to save her brother from embarrassment, mostly hers. Mud wallows, midnight cave checks and one toad-shaped piece of driftwood later, the debunkers come up empty and Linus comes up with a blurry photograph. His sister's parting gift is a pep talk about family quitters, and the search is gloriously back on, because a world with wonder in it needs looking at.

stories.coping: apologizing
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). vocabulary correction (2026-11-12): guilty is ratified; the earlier gap note is obsolete and the tag 'guilty, scared' stands. script_vs_synopsis: the script supplies the conscience machinery, the imagined duck quacking who took my feather, a invented phobia diagnosis, and the twist that the nest was abandoned all along, which is where the guilt-versus-kindness ending lives.
stories.synopsis: Snoopy feels guilty after taking something that isn't his. Embarrassed by a mean nickname, Marcie asks Snoopy for help.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Snoopy's new look needs one finishing touch, a duck feather, freshly borrowed from a duck's nest. Then Lucy paints the victim: some poor duck, cold and sad, quacking where is it? That night the guilty conscience arrives in dreams, and the cure is obvious. Back at the pond the feather goes home, and the pond tells the truth: the nest is long abandoned, the feather was the duck's castoff, and the guilt was optional. Optional, and maybe the point anyway, since returning things you took is what Beagle Scouts do, even when nobody was watching.

stories.synopsis: Snoopy feels guilty after taking something that isn't his. Embarrassed by a mean nickname, Marcie asks Snoopy for help.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Camp bonding day produces nicknames for everyone, and Marcie learns something about herself she never wanted to know: she snores like a buzzsaw. Determined that no living camper will ever hear it, she conscripts Snoopy as a overnight wake-up service, bans herself to the camp office, and ends up broadcast over the loudspeaker anyway, more humiliated than ever. The fix turns out to be the friends: nicknames were supposed to be fun, and if this one isn't, it goes. Keeping them all straight was getting hard anyway, and Marcie heads off, much happier just being Marcie.

stories.synopsis: Emma takes Doug on a beach day to show him why people love it.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Doug has never met a beach, so Emma packs a bag big enough to prove the point: snacks, paddleboards, sandcastles, the works, every activity before sunset. Then Doug notices the strangest beach-goers of all, the ones doing nothing, and learns the one beach activity you don't need equipment for. The day ends at Rebots Beach, where two very busy robot parents learn to unwind, gears going loose.

stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: party-game romp plays 2-4; the accidentally-ruined-by-good-intentions turn and the include-the-left-out-bot coda land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'track down missing supplies' is the mid-episode mystery; the script's spine is Safety Bot's reboot spree, Jenny's friends-are-the-party verdict, and the photo-booth repair.
stories.synopsis: Doug and Emma try to track down missing supplies for a big party.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Jenny Droneberg has made 999 deliveries, and the bots plan to celebrate with a handshake and an early bedtime. Emma has better ideas: limbo, snacks, musical chairs. But Jenny never misses the piñata at all: her thousandth delivery was best celebrated with friends, and the party that survives is part photo shoot, part apology, with Safety Bot right in the frame.

stories.episodeTitle: Vacation Bots / Bots of the Forest
stories.situation: The seaside vacation is fully planned, pool, mini golf, the Super Duper Zuper coaster, the picnic under the stars, and then rain cancels every flight, with Mom rained in on the far side of it. Dad goes quiet doing dishes, and the family's favorite part is the one that got away.
stories.coping: They rebuild the whole vacation at home: hotel pool becomes bathtub pool, mini golf and the coaster become household constructions, and the missed picnic under the stars gets saved by the twinkly lights Doug packed without knowing why. The verdict renames the day: a staycation, because vacations are about having a great time together, not going places.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: home-recreation comedy plays 2-4; the noticed-sadness beat (Dad quiet at the sink) and the together-not-places lesson land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'make a new plan' is the shape; the script supplies the specific recreations, the forgotten-favorite wrinkle, and the packed-lights payoff.
stories.synopsis: When Emma's family vacation is canceled, she and Doug make a new plan.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Emma has the family vacation memorized down to the roller coaster, and the rain cancels all of it: no flights, no hotel pool, no beach picnic, and a mom stuck on the wrong side of the storm. But a Pine family vacation has survived worse. The bathtub becomes the hotel pool, suitcases become the Super Robo Zuper, and when Doug spots Dad's quiet disappointment, the missing piece turns out to be the one Doug accidentally packed: a picnic under twinkly-light stars, and a new word for a vacation that never left the house.

stories.episodeTitle: Vacation Bots / Bots of the Forest
stories.situation: Doug and Bob Bot hike into the woods trusting their robo maps, until a very large moose chases them deep enough that the maps go dead. Officially lost, Dad declares them bots of the forest and starts building a house, and the way home is anything but clear.
stories.coping: Lost and mapless, they still work the problem: retracing steps, then a rescue by hikers Kath and Barb, who teach the whole toolkit, trail blazes, a compass (never eat soggy waffles), the setting sun, and the North Star. Back home, Doug installs a blaze system through the Rebots warehouse so nobody has to be lost to learn it.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: moose-chase and fort-building comedy plays 2-4; the layered wayfinding teaching (blazes, compass, sun, stars) lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'get lost and try to find their way home' is accurate; the script adds Dad's stay-and-settle comedy, the named navigation curriculum, and the blaze-installation coda.
stories.synopsis: Doug and his dad get lost on a hike and try to find their way home.
stories.perStorySynopsis: A hike with Dad starts with moss, wildflowers, and one enormously alarming moose, and ends with two robots genuinely, officially lost, their robo maps dead in the deep woods. Dad copes by declaring a new life in the wilderness, complete with a leaf-TV house, until real hikers Kath and Barb arrive and turn the rescue into a masterclass: trail blazes, a compass, the setting sun, and finally the North Star. Safely home, Doug wires the lesson into the warehouse walls, because every maze, he says, can use a blaze.

stories.situation: A baby duckling turns up in Emma's backyard, far from any pond, and the kids name him Quackerino. Craft-supply homes and a kiddie-pool pond both miss the mark, and the littlest critic stays unhappy in each one.
stories.coping: When Doug's antenna picks up distant quacking, the plan changes from building a home to finding one: waddling like a duck, they lead Quackerino to a real pond and his family. The habitat lesson lands at home plate, an animal's natural home has everything it truly needs, and Doug decides his own favorite habitat is home with his parents.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: quacking, crafting, and waddle-comedy plays 2-4; the habitat-versus-made-home distinction and the goodbye-at-the-pond beat land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'make a new home for a stray duckling' hides that the made homes fail on purpose, twice, before the family reunion gives the real answer.
stories.synopsis: Emma and Doug make a new home for a stray duckling.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Emma's backyard nature shoot finds the most adorable baby duckling either of them has ever seen, and naming him Quackerino is the easy part. The hard part is home: a glitter-dusted craft nest flops, a rebooted kiddie-pool pond with matching lily pads flops harder, and the little duck still is not happy. Then Doug's antenna catches a sound only ducks can answer, and the right move stops being building and starts being leading, waddle by waddle, to a real pond where a whole family is waiting.

stories.situation: Doug and Emma are dragged grocery shopping with a list of must-haves, a deli counter stuck at number 3 while they hold ticket 20, and Mr. Pine promising a mystery surprise. The Swiss cheese wait alone stretches seventeen numbers long, and the race to beat ticket number 20 ends one number short.
stories.coping: The loss flips into the reveal: they were on a scavenger hunt the whole time, and a scavenger hunt is a game where you look for things on a list. The game was the point, not the prize. Doug banks the bigger lesson, anything can be turned into a game, and immediately builds one: an obstacle course that turns Uncle Forkrick's repetitive box-moving job into fun that never shuts down.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: melon-sniffing and basket-shots comedy plays 2-4; the numbers-wait frustration, the one-number miss, and the anything-can-be-a-game reframe land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'errands can be fun' names the moral; the script supplies the deli-ticket race, the scavenger-hunt reveal, the self-checkout surprise, and the Forkrick coda.
stories.synopsis: Emma's dad finds a way to show Emma and Doug how errands can be fun.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Grocery day sounds like the least fun words Doug has ever heard, and Emma agrees until her dad turns the list into a challenge. There are melons to sniff and squeeze, top-shelf baskets to sink from robo-springs, a freezer to brave for froyo, and a deli ticket two numbers from losing it all. When the last item is missed by exactly one ticket number, Mr. Pine lets the secret out: the errand was a scavenger hunt all along, and the surprise at the end is the best one, the self-checkout machine, plus a brand-new game for a very overworked Uncle Forkrick.

When the last item is missed by exactly one ticket number, Mr. Pine lets the secret out: the errand was a scavenger hunt all along, and the surprise at the end is the best one, the self-checkout machine, plus a brand-new game for a very overworked Uncle Forkrick.

stories.situation: Mom's Giz-Go invention escapes and zooms through Rebots, and Doug promised to catch it. Emma reframes the chase as an epic adventure from the Gemstone Joan books, but Doug's imagination is not an app he can download, and the snowcapped mountain she sees is, to his sensors, an ordinary ramp.
stories.coping: Emma teaches the rule that does not need a plug: pretend, don't plug in, and picture something more adventure-y than what you see. The ramp becomes a mountain, the floor becomes lava (safely mopped by Safety Bot), and when the power cuts out, headlamp pretend-work turns a dark warehouse into a tunnel, a runaway mine cart into a catchable target, and a cargo net into the finish of Doug's first real adventure.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: lava-hopping and mine-cart chase plays 2-4; the imagination-lesson meta-craft (pretend, not plug in) and the lose-the-chase-win-the-game structure land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'use his imagination while looking for a lost item' is the frame; the script adds the pretend-not-plug-in teaching, the Safety Bot interlude, and the mom's jungle-weeding coda.
stories.synopsis: Emma shows Doug how to use his imagination while looking for a lost item.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Doug promised to catch his mom's runaway Giz-Go, and Emma has decided the chase counts as an adventure, Gemstone Joan hats and all. One problem: Doug cannot see the mountains she sees, because imagination is not an app. Then the lesson takes, a ramp becomes a peak, a floor becomes lava, and a blackout becomes a tunnel chase with a runaway mine cart. By the time the cargo net comes down, Doug has caught the invention, earned the name adventure buddy, and left his mom wondering why weeding the garden suddenly feels like a jungle expedition.

stories.episodeTitle: Bot on the Farm / Bot-Cycle Built for Two
stories.situation: Armed with a library book and a full plug-in download, Doug and Emma declare themselves the Farming Dream Team and take over the farm for the day, right up until a robo-vacuum mangles the blueberry patch and the cows simply will not listen, then bolt entirely.
stories.coping: Nana and Grandbot take the runaway-cow disaster gently: you are not supposed to know everything, and some things can only be learned by doing, over time, with experience. They hand over their earned tricks (a special sound, an ear scratch, following the food), and Doug's new digi-book leaves pages deliberately blank, because there is always more to learn.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: blueberry-vacuum and cow-chase slapstick plays 2-4; the knowing-versus-experience lesson and the blank-pages coda land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'learn about farming' hides the know-it-all setup, the two failures, and the grandbots' experience lesson that reframes the whole visit.
stories.synopsis: Doug and Emma learn about farming while visiting Doug's grandbots.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Doug and Emma arrive at the grandbots' farm knowing everything there is to know, one from a book, one from a download, and volunteer to run the place for the day. The blueberries fight back, the apples need actual tools, and the cows go rogue at full speed. The rescue comes from the farmers who have been at this for years, and their secret is not a fact at all: some things you can only learn by doing. The pie gets baked, the cows get milked, and Doug's new digi-book goes home with blank pages on purpose.

stories.episodeTitle: Bot on the Farm / Bot-Cycle Built for Two
stories.situation: Emma teaches Doug to ride his new bike in four steps, pedaling, balancing, steering, stopping, and it is going perfectly until Emma takes a fall. The bot who never falls is suddenly the one too scared to get back on, and she hides it so she will not stop Doug from riding.
stories.coping: Critter Bot quietly relays Emma's secret, and Doug does not tease or push: he names it, offers the out, then gives exactly the help she asks for. With a steadying hand and a five-count eject, the lightning is back on the thunder, and the teacher thanks the student for getting her back on her bike.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: bike-training montage plays 2-4; the fear-after-a-fall beat, hiding it to protect someone else, and the role reversal land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'he tries learning how to ride' is half the story; the script's heart is Emma's fall, her hidden fear, and the student-becomes-teacher ending.
stories.synopsis: When Doug sees Emma's bike, he tries learning how to ride.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Doug has a shiny new bike called the Robo-Racer and a teacher who has never fallen, which makes the lesson look easy until it happens to her instead. One spill and Emma is done, secretly scared, and quietly steering Doug toward riding alone so he will not stop. Critter Bot has other ideas, and soon the student is doing the steadying: a held bike, a countdown, and the wind back in Emma's gears, with both of them agreeing the day needed the other one.
