stories.episodeTitle: Eva's Big Catch / Carlos's Juice Stand
stories.situation: Carlos needs someone to run his beloved juice stand for one night, and Eva volunteers with an upgrade in mind: more kinds of juice than his one blueberry. To fit them all in, she skips his steps one by one, the tasting, the full press, the pine sap, until the stand is serving cran-pepper-anchovy delight and the customers are gone.
stories.coping: Carlos comes back from his grandma's and diagnoses it kindly: all the steps are important, and they took him a long time, and a lot of blech, to figure out. One new juice, made together with every step kept, becomes Happy Sappy Peachberry Juice, the customers return, and Eva's diary credits the whole thing to doing all of the steps.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: wild-flavor comedy plays 2-4; the shortcut-costs-customers arc and the steps-were-earned lesson land 5-7. emotion drawn from the ratified 18-term list (impatience added 2026-11-11). script_vs_synopsis: 'shakes things up' names the experiment; the script supplies the step-skipping cascade, the empty-stand low, and Carlos's blech backstory.
stories.synopsis: Eva shakes things up at the local juice stand.
stories.perStorySynopsis: One night behind Carlos's juice stand is not enough time for Eva to serve his way, so she speeds up: more flavors, fewer steps, no tasting, a little less pressing, who needs the pine sap anyway. The customers get surprises like cherry-pepper and blueberry onion, and they vote with their wings. Carlos returns from his grandmother's to an empty stand and a confession, and instead of scolding, he shares how long his steps took to earn, then invites one new juice, made properly, together. Happy Sappy Peachberry Juice brings everybody back.

stories.situation: Eva's first sleepover runs on a list of super-duper plans, and the plans fail in order: no clouds for cloud-watching, paper too wet to paint, and Baby Mo finds the treasure-hunt pine cone before the hunt begins. While Eva scrambles to the next idea, her guests are playing, and she almost misses a whole sleepover of fun happening without her.
stories.coping: The reveal arrives in the guests' own voices: daytime leaf-jumping is super-duper, and this is the most fun sleepover ever. Eva's diary does the honest math, it did not matter that her plans were not super or duper, because her friends know how to have fun and do not need her to make it for them. She joins the game she was busy managing, and the late-arriving clouds get written into a cloudy story.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: plan-flop comedy plays 2-4; the hosting anxiety, the missed-fun reveal, and the friends-are-already-fun lesson land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'hosts her first sleepover' hides the plan-by-plan collapse, the literal it's-hopeless low, and the fun-was-happening-without-me turn.
stories.synopsis: Eva hosts her first sleepover.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Eva has planned her first sleepover down to the leaf piles, and the universe declines to cooperate: cloudless skies, wet watercolors, and a baby brother who wins the treasure hunt solo. Convinced the whole night is a disaster, Eva keeps rushing to the next plan while her guests laugh without her. The rescue is not a plan at all, it is the discovery that the sleepover has been fun the entire time, and the hostess finally jumps into the leaf pile she was too busy to notice.

stories.situation: Lantern day at school should be Lucy's showcase, but her blackberry-paint idea sends Eva recruiting her for Carlos, Sue, Jacob, and Kiera, one classmate at a time, without ever asking Lucy first. Eva's own sky lantern stays blank until Lucy, out of time for her Springtime Wonder-lantern, finally says she cannot help right now, and Eva cannot understand why.
stories.coping: Lucy explains it plainly: she spent all her time on everyone else's lanterns and now has none for her own. Eva owns the pattern, I should have asked you before I said yes for you, hands over her own petals, and solves her stars herself with a twig and a what-would-Lucy-do. Lucy gets the switch, the thanks, and the choice next time, because helping is hers to give.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: lantern-decorating plays 2-4; the volunteering-someone-else's-time arc, the apology, and the helping-is-her-choice lesson land 5-7. vocabulary gap: Eva's dominant felt state after the no is guilt, which is not on the 18-term list, so tagged confused/embarrassed as nearest. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis states the interruption pattern; the script adds the blank-lantern cost, the first-no moment, and Eva's self-reliance turn.
stories.synopsis: Lucy's art making keeps getting interrupted by Eva asking her to help other owlets.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Ms. Featherbottom's lantern project turns the class into artists, and Lucy into the most in-demand idea bank in Treetopington, because Eva keeps offering her services to whoever needs one. By the time the lanterns are due, everyone else's glows and the Springtime Wonder-lantern is bare, and the friend who says no for the first time is the one being told she is not helping. Eva repairs it the Lucy way: return the petals, poke her own stars with a twig, and hand the honor of lighting the class tree to the owlet who lit everyone else's.

stories.situation: Dad's new Pine Forest route means later nights, and the first casualty is pinecone pizza night. Eva wakes him before sunrise to speed the route, hurries him past snack breaks, dumps a whole bag of mail, and still loses the race with sunset, hearing her dad apologize for being too late.
stories.coping: Sorting the scattered mail shows Eva what the route actually carries, a pan flute from a sister, a hatchday present, a postcard from grandowlets, in other words, presents, music, and happiness. The plan flips from getting Dad home to giving back: while he finishes, the family builds a lumpy, peppery pinecone pizza thingy, and Dad declares it better than his because everybody made it.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: dropped-mail and lumpy-pizza comedy plays 2-4; the what-does-Dad's-work-mean realization and the role-reversal dinner land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'helps her dad work faster' is the engine; the script adds the mail catastrophe, the happiness discovery, and the family-cooks-for-Dad reversal. retagged: 'disappointed, kind' to 'disappointed, proud' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed). vibe provisional: drafted as warm, mapped to the guide's calm/silly/energetic vocabulary (vibe rule undecided).
stories.synopsis: Anxiously awaiting pinecone pizza night, Eva helps her dad work faster.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Pinecone pizza night is sacred, and Dad's longer mail route is threatening it, so Eva becomes his delivery partner, sunrise wake-up and all. The speed run scatters mail across the forest and the pizza across the evening, and somewhere in the pickup Eva reads what she has been delivering, music, presents, and happiness for owls who need it. Dad flies home to a pizza made by the family he feeds all day, lumpy with too much pepper, and better than his, he says, for exactly that reason.

stories.situation: One seed-catching save puts Eva on the front page of the Treetopington Times, and one headline stops feeling like enough. She chases the next story, owlball over the world's largest pine cone, acorn stacking, both crash, and then she hands the paper a better story, Sue and Carlos's brand-new pumpkin seed bread, and feels the small honest ache: I wish the story was about me.
stories.coping: Watching her shared story work, the whole town baking the recipe, teaches the reframe: what goes in the paper are stories that make owls' lives better, not stories about being seen. The ache gets said out loud to Mom, and it gets outgrown in the same scene as Eva recommends Lucy's dance for the next front page.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: acorn-stacking and headline comedy plays 2-4; the enough-vs-more arc, the named envy, and the share-the-story turn land 5-7. vocabulary gap: the confession is closest to envy, not on the 18-term list, so tagged disappointed/excited as nearest. script_vs_synopsis: 'winds up on the front page' undersells the second-fame chase, the two failed stunts, and the generosity resolution. retagged: 'disappointed, excited' to 'disappointed, proud' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed).
stories.synopsis: Eva winds up on the front page of the town newspaper.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Eva saves a jar of seeds and lands on the front page, and suddenly one headline feels like a habit to keep. The stunts get bigger and the landings get harder, and the newsstand stays Eva-less. Then a whiff of pumpkin seed bread shows her the better story, one that makes the whole town's life tastier, and she gives it to the paper herself. The front page belongs to Sue and Carlos this time, and the owlet who shared it discovers the part that never gets old, reading about friends.

stories.coping: The synopsis points to the resolution shape: Eva helps the lost oriole look for his family, and the search becomes a lesson in what community means, a town showing up for one lost bird. Specific beats and the exact resolution are not verifiable this pass.

stories.situation: Toad bakes the best cookies he has ever made, and he and Frog keep needing one very, very last bite. Every willpower scheme leaks: the box gets a string, the string gets untied, the shelf gets a ladder, the outside gets a hole with robins standing by, and the river gets a raft headed for the falls.
stories.coping: The victory is giving the whole batch to the robins, and the honesty keeps going: Frog announces they now have lots and lots of willpower, Toad mutters that Frog can keep it, he is going home to bake a cake. Self-control is hard, trying hard not to do what you really want to do, and the show lets the joke land without pretending otherwise.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: one-more-bite comedy plays 2-4; naming willpower and watching every scheme fail lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'try to resist' is the arc; the script supplies the escalating hide-the-box schemes, the raft finale, and the bake-a-cake punchline.
stories.synopsis: Frog and Toad try to resist a batch of yummy cookies.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Toad has baked his greatest cookies ever, which is exactly the problem: neither he nor Frog can stop at one very last bite, or the next one. Willpower, they learn, is trying hard not to do something you really want to do, and it is tested by strings, ladders, holes, helpful robins, and a cookie raft bound for a waterfall. The last idea is the one that works, and the friends end the day cookie-less, willpower-rich, and already planning a cake.

stories.situation: Toad's sad time of day is sitting on the porch waiting for mail that never comes, not even on his birthday, because in his whole life no one has ever sent him a letter. Frog hears it and leaves with something he must do, then spends the walk to town telling every neighbor it is Toad's very first letter.
stories.coping: Frog fixes the sad time of day at the source, a first letter that says what a best friend should, mailed by the slowest courier available so the suspense is real (and half given away early). The mailbox overflows with the town's follow-up mail, and Toad's verdict lands on the one that matters: he likes Frog's letter best.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: snail-mail comedy plays 2-4; the sad-time-of-day setup and the being-thought-of payoff land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'writes Toad a letter' is the plot; the script adds the sad-time-of-day frame, the town's first-letter anecdotes, the secret blurted early, and the whole-town avalanche. retagged: 'sad, kind' to 'sad, lonely' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed).
stories.synopsis: Frog finds out Toad has never gotten mail before, so he writes Toad a letter.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Every day has a sad time for Toad: porch-sitting, mailbox-watching, and mail that never comes, not even on birthdays. Frog's answer is a letter of his own, written until it is just right, then handed to a snail with instructions for speed that the snail has never possessed. By the time the letter arrives, the whole town has added to the pile, and Toad, holding his first mail ever, sorts through poems, recipes, and coupons to find the one he likes best, from his best friend.

stories.situation: Toad cannot choose from Mink's enormous flavor list, so he orders one scoop of every flavor for Frog and himself, then walks home under the hot sun while the tower melts over his eyes. Covered in sticks, leaves, and drips, he becomes the scary thing everyone is fleeing, including a Frog who cannot fly away because he promised to wait right here.
stories.coping: Toad's confession, I have ruined everything, gets met exactly right: Frog names the kindness behind the accident, you wanted to do something nice for us, and solves the melting with a walk instead of a wait. They eat the ice cream at the stand the moment it is scooped, two chocolate cones, no melting, no waiting, and both are glad the scary thing was Toad.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: melting-cone monster comedy plays 2-4; the ruined-gift guilt and the kindness-behind-the-accident line land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'melty disaster' is the midpoint; the script adds the one-of-every-flavor decision, the monster-on-the-path panic, and the eat-it-at-the-stand fix.
stories.synopsis: Toad's delivery of refreshing ice cream to Frog turns into a melty disaster.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Choosing one flavor is impossible for Toad, so he chooses all of them, a towering gift for Frog on a blazing hot day. The walk home goes badly one drip at a time until a cone-covered Toad becomes the monster of the meadow, pursued by everyone he likes. When the truth and the puddle are revealed, Frog does what best friends do, spots the kindness inside the accident, and finds the one fix that beats the sun: ice cream eaten exactly where it is scooped.

stories.situation: Toad's favorite jacket loses a button on a walk, and only the exact button will do: the search retraces the whole day, through the sneezy meadow, the dark woods, and the river, turning up buttons that are black, two-holed, small, and square, everything except his. Toad declares they will never find it while Frog refuses to quit.
stories.coping: The answer is anticlimactic and true: the button has been on Toad's floor the whole time. He does the repair properly, returning the found buttons, sewing on his own, then handing Frog the jacket itself with every button sewn extra tight, because you are my favorite friend. The day ends with two friends choosing a walk, buttons intact.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: wrong-button comedy plays 2-4; the search-fatigue low and the give-the-jacket apology land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'great lengths' is the engine; the script adds the four wrong-button tests, the whole-world-covered-with-buttons low, and the jacket gift.
stories.synopsis: Frog and Toad go to great lengths to find a lost button.
stories.perStorySynopsis: A missing button on a favorite jacket sends Frog and Toad back over every step of their day, and every finding is wrong: too black, too few holes, too small, too square. The world, Toad concludes, is covered in buttons, none of them his, and the search ends the way hard days do, at home, where the button has been on the floor all along. What Toad does with the relief is the story: a jacket handed over with its buttons sewn on extra tight, for the friend who never stopped looking.

stories.situation: The most beautiful first day of spring ever is passing while Toad sleeps straight through it, and Frog is lonely without him. Toad counters every invitation with half past spring, a time that does not exist, and Frog has already proven he is excellent at waiting.
stories.coping: Waiting alone loses to a small forgivable fraud: Frog tears the calendar pages so it reads half past spring, and Toad, convinced, gets up and out. On the walk he works out the truth, it is not really half past spring, and forgives it instantly, it is still very beautiful, and I am glad you got me out of bed.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: bed-pushing and calendar comedy plays 2-4; the loneliness of missing a friend, the trick, and Toad's graceful catch of it land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Frog wants Toad to spend the first day of spring with him' hides the wait-all-day structure, the calendar fraud, and Toad's seeing-through-it ending. retagged: 'lonely, hopeful' to 'lonely, frustrated' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed).
stories.synopsis: Frog wants Toad to spend the first day of spring with him.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Spring arrives in full glory, and Toad greets it from under a blanket, negotiating for half past spring, a time that is not on any clock. Frog waits beautifully, then waits badly, tearing calendar pages to make the impossible time arrive. Out on the meadow, Toad notices the cold, then the calendar, then the truth, and lets him off entirely: it is still very beautiful, and being woken into spring with a friend was worth the trick.

stories.situation: A story about brave Sir Toad and brave Squire Frog raises the question, are we brave? and the test is the tippy top of Mount Gloom, climbed without an umbrella, on a day of dark caves, glowing yellowish eyes, and rocks that tumble bigger and bigger.
stories.coping: Each scare gets answered the way the book heroes would, together: we are not afraid, mostly truthfully, with the cave and its lonely monster behind them. At the top, brave is confirmed, and the punchline is asking to be brave back at Toad's house, where two friends shelter from the storm they climbed into, feeling very brave together.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: cave-and-rock comedy plays 2-4; the are-we-brave question, pretending-not-afraid, and the sheltering-together ending land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'to prove they're brave' is the setup; the script adds the story-within-story, the cave monster, and the run-for-dessert retreat.
stories.synopsis: To prove they're brave, Frog and Toad set off to climb Mount Gloom.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Frog and Toad read about brave Sir Toad and brave Squire Frog and wonder the obvious: are we brave? The test writes itself, the tippy top of Mount Gloom, no umbrella, in the rain. There are dark caves (one occupied by a monster who mostly wanted company), rocks that tumble bigger and bigger, and wind that is too windy, and the two keep answering it the story way, together, we are not afraid. The summit certifies their bravery just in time for them to run back down and be brave indoors, where the cocoa is.

stories.situation: Toad plants his very first seeds and meets the gap between quite soon and now: nothing grows. He shouts instructions underground, decides the seeds are afraid, of the dark, then of the rain, and works through the whole comfort catalogue, firefly night lights, stories in the rain, poetry, silly faces, and a full hootenanny.
stories.coping: Morning brings green: the sprouts are up. Frog floats the gentle correction, maybe they were not afraid, maybe they just needed time to grow, and Toad reframes his waiting as work: he kept them company, read them stories, played them music. A gardener is born, and he is off to find a tuba for the garden.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: shouting-at-seeds comedy plays 2-4; the waiting-versus-doing lesson and the reframed hard work land 5-7. emotion drawn from the ratified 18-term list (impatience added 2026-11-11). script_vs_synopsis: 'thinks the seeds are afraid' is Toad's theory; the script supplies the quite-soon confusion, the full care-ritual catalogue, and the time-to-grow reveal.
stories.synopsis: Toad thinks the seeds in his new garden are afraid to grow.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Toad plants his first garden with total confidence and zero patience, and the seeds respond to neither. Clearly they are afraid: of the dark (firefly disco), of the rain (bedtime stories), of silence (poems, songs, silly faces). When the sprouts finally arrive, so does the quieter truth, the seeds were not scared, they were growing at seed speed. Toad hears it, keeps his version too, and marches off to buy a tuba, because a garden this well cared for deserves music.

stories.situation: Rabbit's cake smells wonderful but is for a very special day, Tuesday, and waiting a whole day is impossible. Frog invents Frog Bakes a Cake for Toad Day and bakes with total confidence and no skill: eggs with shells, milk floods, sugar chaos, while Toad watches, wincing, and finally says the hard thing.
stories.coping: The confession, I do not know how to bake a cake, is met with joy instead of mockery: Toad takes over and does it together, until Frog names the takeover, it cannot be Frog Bakes a Cake for Toad Day when Toad bakes the cake. Toad makes it right with his own strange, hard, not-very-sweet cake, and Frog calls it the best he has ever had, a cake he will always remember.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: shell-egg and lumpy-batter comedy plays 2-4; the kind-failure confession, the taken-over feeling named out loud, and the remembered-cake ending land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'even though he doesn't know how' is the setup; the script adds the Tuesday obsession, the full baking disaster, and the mutual cake preference swap. retagged: 'embarrassed, kind' to 'embarrassed, frustrated' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed).
stories.synopsis: Frog wants to bake a cake for Toad, even though he doesn't know how.
stories.perStorySynopsis: One whiff of Rabbit's Tuesday cake sends Frog to the kitchen on a mission of love, Frog Bakes a Cake for Toad Day, though his recipe knowledge ends at the word flour. Shells in the bowl, milk over the rim, sugar everywhere, and a guest of honor trying very hard to be polite. The day gets rescued by honesty in both directions: Frog admits he cannot bake, Toad admits being taken over does not feel like together, and the lumpy cake they share ends up the best either has ever had.

stories.situation: A homemade kite, a field of robin critics, and a wind that has to be summoned by licking a finger: the first flights crash, and Toad absorbs the verdict that the kite lacks aerodynamics and might as well be thrown away. Frog keeps prescribing confidence, plus running, waving, and shouting up, kite, up.
stories.coping: The very, very last try works, and the kite's reward is dragging both friends into the sky. The rescue chain grows one neighbor at a time until Frog declares the real decision: the kite goes on its adventure without them, everyone lets go on the count of three, and the pair land on the honest summary, flying it took work, confidence, and running and shouting and jumping, and it was fun. Only a little bit of fun.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: kite-crash and dog-walked-by-kite comedy plays 2-4; the doubters-versus-confidence arc and the letting-go ending land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'despite some doubting Robins' names the hecklers; the script adds the summon-the-wind bit, the whole-town rescue chain, and the deliberate let-go.
stories.synopsis: Frog and Toad attempt to fly their homemade kite despite some doubting Robins.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Frog has confidence in the homemade kite, Toad has a face full of meadow, and the robins have notes: too heavy, too many holes, no aerodynamics. After every crash there is one more very, very last try, and the try that works lifts them both clean off the ground. The kite, it turns out, also has confidence, and a whole neighborhood grabs the string before Frog and Toad choose the ending they want, letting go, so the kite can reach the top of the sky on its own.

stories.situation: A walk on the wrong path leaves Frog and Toad lost in the woods. Toad cycles through what to do, what to do, and misses lunch in the forecast, while Gopher asks the perfect unhelpful question: do you not know where you are, or not know where you are going?
stories.coping: Frog does not pretend the feeling away, he re-names the day: explorers. The unusual way turns out to be blueberries tested for safety, a babbling brook, a nap in the grass, and maple seeds spinning, and by dusk Toad thanks him for a pleasant afternoon. The exit line carries the whole lesson: you are never truly lost when you are with a friend.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: lost-in-the-woods comedy plays 2-4; the staying-calm attempt, the explorer reframe, and the friend-is-the-answer line land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'handles being lost differently' is the contrast; the script adds the two-kinds-of-lost Gopher gag, the explorer conversion, and the never-truly-lost close.
stories.synopsis: Frog handles being lost differently than Toad.
stories.perStorySynopsis: One unfamiliar tree later, Frog and Toad are officially lost, and each is lost in his own way: Toad catastrophizing toward a missed lunch, Frog staying calm with visible effort. Then comes the reframe, explorers do not get lost, they discover, and the woods deliver blueberries, a brook, a grassy nap, and spinning maple seeds. Home finds them by dark, as home does, with Toad refusing a repeat tomorrow and keeping the lovely day anyway, because with a friend you are never truly lost.

stories.situation: Frog is in bed looking quite green, even for a frog, and asks for a made-up story, and Toad has nothing. The hunt goes everywhere: porch pacing, flowerpot searching, pump-splashing, story-shouting, head-standing to shake stories loose, and a full hop-jump-skip-flip routine down the big hill.
stories.coping: Toad returns exhausted and green to find Frog recovered, who retires the request, thanks him for giving it such a good try, and then tells Toad one: the story of a toad who could not think of a story, performed exactly as it just happened, ending with the toad tucked into bed. Failure becomes the story, and being cared for gets returned in kind.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: shake-the-stories-loose comedy plays 2-4; the caring-until-you-drop arc and the story-of-the-day-itself land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'tries everything' is the shape; the script adds each specific failed method, the role reversal, and the story-within-the-story ending.
stories.synopsis: Toad tries everything to think of a story to tell his sick friend.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Frog is sick and wants only one thing, a story made up out of Toad's imagination, which turns out to be the one thing in the world Toad cannot find. He walks, searches, pumps, shouts, stands on his head, and tumbles down a hill, and comes home empty, dizzy, and green even for a toad. Frog, feeling better, hands the favor back: a story about a toad who could not think of a story, told gently to the friend asleep in his bed.

stories.situation: Toad's mind is filled with everything he has to do, so on Dragonfly's advice he makes a list, and the list becomes the boss: swimming is not on the list, blueberries are not on the list, and letting Frog cross something off is certainly not on the list. Then the wind takes the paper, and running after it is not on the list either.
stories.coping: Frog runs for the list because he has no list, and when it is gone forever, Toad finds the graceful answer: he cannot remember what else was on it, so the only thing to do is sit and do nothing. The day ends with the last item crossed out, go to sleep, and one list amendment from Frog: say good night.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: list-boss comedy plays 2-4; the rigidity-versus-friendship arc, the lost-list crisis, and the doing-nothing resolution land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'blows away in the wind' is the turn; the script adds the list-gags, the not-on-my-list refusals, and the sit-and-do-nothing ending.
stories.synopsis: Toad writes a list of things to do, which blows away in the wind.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Overwhelmed by a busy day, Toad writes a list and discovers the strange comfort of crossing things off, wake up, make breakfast, go to Frog's house. The list starts ruling the day, blocking swims, blueberries, and even a kind Frog holding a pen. When the wind steals it, the crisis dissolves into the best idea yet: with the list gone, there is nothing to do but sit together and do nothing, then cross off go to sleep and add say good night.

stories.situation: Mink's brand-new shoes make Toad want to run fast, jump high, and have lots of fun too, so he buys the last pair at Squirrel's shop and forces them on a size too small. He spends the whole walk insisting they are perfectly fine while they squeak, trip him, and finally land Frog in the mud.
stories.coping: The honest moment arrives on a mud bank: I thought I wanted new shoes, but now I just feel silly, and my feet hurt. Frog's gentle logic reframes them, they were new when you left the store, now they are old shoes, and old shoes he does not need. Toad frees his toes, gives the shoes and their laces to Robin, and rediscovers that his own bare feet walk exactly as fast as he wants.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: too-small-shoe comedy plays 2-4; the wanting-what-someone-else-has arc and the I-feel-silly admission land 5-7. vocabulary gap: Toad's opening pull is envy, not on the 18-term list, so tagged embarrassed/disappointed as nearest. script_vs_synopsis: 'just to be like everyone else' is the motive; the script adds the size-too-small squeeze, the mud fall, and the old-shoes-now reasoning.
stories.synopsis: Toad buys a pair of new shoes just to be like everyone else.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Mink has new shoes, everyone wants to see them, and suddenly Toad does too, never mind that toads do not wear shoes. The purchase fits like a mistake, squeaks like one, and costs him a whole morning of pretending. The release is two-part, admitting the shoes were for looking like Mink rather than for walking like Toad, and gifting them onward, before the best discovery of the day: his own bare feet can wiggle, run, and jump just fine.

stories.situation: A quiet night in is interrupted by the discovery that Toad's special-occasion jacket has sat alone in the dark of the closet for a very long time. The remedy is a manufactured occasion, a night on the town, for the jacket, that escalates through puddle splashes, a rowboat, a swim, every soup on the menu, and a dance that ends in a rip.
stories.coping: The jacket gets its night, and the wearers get theirs, exhausted. The closing arithmetic is the lesson: it was a special occasion, next time the jacket stays home, and the found slippers turn an ordinary night in into exactly the occasion they wanted. Special things, the story suggests, are allowed out on ordinary nights.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: soup-party and dance comedy plays 2-4; the saving-things-for-someday idea and the quiet-night-in payoff land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the jacket premise is new from the script (no catalog synopsis beyond the title pair); the escalation chain and slippers ending are script evidence.
stories.synopsis: Frog helps Toad give his special jacket a night on the town.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Frog goes hunting for slippers and finds instead a fancy jacket that has been waiting years in the dark for a special occasion that never comes. stories.situation: Harriet breaks her own no-school-spying rule to stake out Agatha K. Plumber, a lawyer so scared of starting her new life that she has not left her bed in months. Harriet wants to witness history, and instead gets caught by dogs in pants and thrown out, and blows every appointment Mrs. Plumber had lined up.
stories.coping: Harriet wants to quit, then quotes her own rule back at herself, life is a struggle and a good spy never quits. She deputizes Janie and Sport to rebuild the schedule (a hair emergency, a bank meeting) and walks back into the building she was thrown out of, turning a caught spy into the nudge Mrs. Plumber needed.
stories.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis does not show the dogs-in-pants capture, the rebuilt appointment chain, or that Harriet's spying is what pushes Mrs. Plumber out of bed. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Harriet's ambition to know and see everything may change reclusive Agatha K. Plumber's life for the better.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harriet M. Welsch puts reclusive Agatha K. Plumber on her spy route and discovers the lawyer quit her job to open a doggy clothing store, then got so scared of the risk she never gets out of bed. When Harriet sneaks in to witness the big first step, the dogs spot her, the housekeeper throws her out, and the whole day of appointments collapses. A good spy never quits, so Harriet recruits Janie and Sport to rebuild the schedule, marches back into the belly of the beast, and watches Mrs. Plumber finally walk out the door toward her new life.

stories.situation: The day before Ole Golly turns 35, Harriet finds her childhood to-do list with items unchecked, including learn to ride a bike, and turns the birthday into a mission to finish the list in one day. Ole Golly keeps going weird and evasive, and Harriet cannot tell what the list really means to her.
stories.coping: Harriet pushes until Ole Golly admits her secret: she chickens out of anything big and scary, and she is afraid to take the risk on her bookstore dream. Harriet points to the one death-defying item Ole Golly already pulled off, helping Harriet grow up, which turns out to mean learning to ride the bike with her eyes up, looking where she wants to go, and planting the tree now.
stories.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis keeps the list frame; the script supplies the bike lesson in the park, the marry-Ole-Golly recruiting subplot, the grumpy bookstore owner's warning, and Ole Golly's confession about chickening out. confidence high. catalog synopsis restructured to remove dashes.
stories.synopsis: On her birthday, Ole Golly revisits a list of everything she wanted to do by the age of 35, and Harriet is determined to help her complete it.
stories.perStorySynopsis: A letter from Ole Golly's mother arrives holding a list she wrote as a girl: everything to accomplish by 35, with items still unchecked, including learn to ride a bike. Harriet commandeers the birthday eve to finish the list, teaching her nanny to ride while friends scout unlikely husbands, and a discouraging bookstore owner nearly undoes the day. Then Ole Golly confesses her dirty little secret, she chickens out of big, scary things, and Harriet shows her the one practically death-defying item she already did: raising Harriet. Back on the bike with her eyes up, Ole Golly decides the second-best time to plant a tree is now, and walks into a bookstore to finally begin.

stories.situation: Harriet finds the one coat that is completely her, and Marion Hawthorne claims Harriet copied her, forcing a class vote over who gets to wear it. Harriet has never beaten Marion at anything, and half the class votes out of fear.
stories.coping: Harriet digs for proof Marion is lying about only owning one coat, then reframes the vote as bigger than the coat: a stand for Pinky Whitehead and everyone Marion pushes around. She hijacks the morning announcements, and the scared kids find they can say out loud what they never dared.
stories.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis holds the vote; the script shows the Beth Ellen rope-bell proof hunt, Harriet's torn old coat as a story, and the announcements broadcast that flips the frightened voters. confidence high. catalog synopsis restructured to remove dashes.
stories.synopsis: Harriet's new coat is perfect for her, and apparently for Marion Hawthorne too. But who will win the school's vote?
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harriet's new navy peacoat is perfect, silent as a shadow, collar up like Jack London, until Marion Hawthorne declares it is hers and demands a class vote. Harriet digs up proof that Marion's my-search-is-over single coat is a lie with Beth Ellen's help, andBill the journalist wants more than two dings on a rope bell. Caught snooping in Marion's closet, Harriet realizes the vote is really about every kid Marion has bullied. On the morning announcements she calls the vote what it is, freedom, and the class that always obeyed Marion starts saying so out loud.

stories.episodeTitle: Cross My Heart and Hope Not to Dance
stories.situation: Harriet and Janie's sacred oath to never attend dancing school starts cracking when their mothers sign them up, and worse, Harriet discovers Janie secretly likes dancing. When the instructor insists only boys may lead, Harriet revolts, and the oath book becomes the battleground.
stories.coping: Harriet drags Sport in as keeper of the oaths to invalidate the counter-oath, then faces the real choice: keep a rule that says girls can never lead, or let the oath go. She chooses the cause over the rule, throws off the gloves, and dances the revolution with everyone, no partner rules.
stories.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis is the setup only; the script shows the oath/counter-oath/counter-counter-oath machinery, the girls-can't-lead confrontation, and Janie's admission she never hated dancing, she had just never tried it. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Janie and Harriet vow never to go to dancing school, but Harriet doesn't know that Janie actually likes dancing.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harriet and Janie swore a sacred oath in kindergarten: never, ever, ever attend dancing school. Their mothers finally outflank them, and at class Harriet discovers the real betrayal, Janie is smiling and admits she actually likes dancing because she never tried it. Then Mr. Dubois rules that girls must follow because boys are bigger, and Harriet decides no oath is worth defending that. With Sport reading the oath book's fine print, the counter-oath collapses, the gloves come off, and Harriet leads a no-rules dancing revolution.

stories.situation: Harriet has a run-everything-wrong day: no dime for the subway, broken plates, grounded, and her two best friends mad at her. She decides the answer is to be truly alone and takes the cat-sitting job at Mr. Withers's apartment with its 26 cats, shutting her friends out mid-science-project.
stories.coping: Alone in the dark with nothing to write about, Harriet learns that peace turns to loneliness fast, and when Ole Golly arrives with her worried friends, she lets them in. The team effort of catching 26 escaped cats opens Mr. Withers's shut door to his estranged brother too, and Harriet concludes the trick is letting the world in.
stories.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis stops at the doubt about alone time; the script shows the space-mission imagination, the blackout fear, the man in the brown fedora being the brother, and the let-the-world-in conclusion. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: After an awful day, Harriet wants some alone time. Watching Mr. Withers' 26 cats is just what she needs...or is it?
stories.perStorySynopsis: The world has it in for Harriet, so she takes Mr. Withers's cat-sitting job and plans to be truly alone, truly at peace, as she imagines it, a lone cosmonaut with 26 cats named Bobbys, Tommys, and Geraldines. She ditches Janie and Sport mid-science-project, and the peace curdles: a blackout, cat food for dinner, nothing left to write about. When a knock turns out to be her friends worried and the feared animal-control man is really Mr. Withers's estranged brother, the cat escape turns into a neighborhood rescue, and Harriet figures out that being alone all the way is just being lonely. The trick is letting the world in.

stories.situation: On new-notebook day, Harriet discovers her birth certificate records her middle name as a scribble, and what she thought was a cool mysterious M might be nothing at all. She swipes the document from City Hall, gets caught, and decides she cannot trust even her parents or Ole Golly.
stories.coping: Ole Golly takes Harriet to meet her own mother, whose naming fight (Willa versus Myrtle) has run for decades, and shows her the shelf of books behind her chosen name. Harriet discovers identity is something you write: she adopts Myrtle for a day to heal the fight, keeps Harriet M. Welsch for real, and forgives her parents because even parents make mistakes, and mistakes give you great stories.
stories.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis skims the identity lesson; the script supplies the City Hall heist, Ole Golly's mother in Far Rockaway, the Willa Cather backstory behind Willa's bookstore, and the M question mark to M period arc. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Harriet learns about her middle initial and questions who she is. Her nanny, Ole Golly, teaches Harriet a valuable lesson about identity.
stories.perStorySynopsis: New notebook day goes wrong when Harriet learns her official middle name is a scribble, not the magnificent M she has been signing. She swipes her birth certificate from City Hall, lands in trouble with her parents and in a sulk with Ole Golly, who responds by taking her to meet her own mother. There a decades-long name fight (Willa, invented; Myrtle, inherited) shows Harriet that names are chosen as much as given, and Ole Golly's bookshelf shows what a person can build behind the name she picks. Harriet keeps Harriet M. Welsch, but now she knows what the M stands for, and she forgives her parents, because even parents make mistakes, and mistakes make great stories.

stories.situation: Harriet gets VIP access to her idol Vic Lancer through her TV-producer dad, then learns the song that means everything to her was written by Louis Redd, the guitarist Vic takes credit for. The star also has stage fright and a fried-pickle demand, and the show may not go on.
stories.coping: Harriet first wants to confront Vic, then hears Louis explain the unfairness he cannot fix yet, and Janie helps her see the step-by-step reality behind her outrage. She saves the show with Ole Golly's tomato sandwich made with love, gets Louis his on-air credit, and lets the friendship catch the complicated truth together.
stories.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis names only the discovery; the script shows the backstage chaos, the fried-pickle standoff, the ventriloquist's-dummy argument, and the Janie-Harriet conversation about fairness and moving step by step. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Janie and Harriet get to meet their favorite singer, only to discover a shocking truth about his music.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harriet's dad scores her VIP tickets to Vic Lancer, the singer whose song Gone, Gone, Gone feels written just for her. Backstage she meets the real writer, Louis Redd, a road musician missing his family, while Vic barricades himself in his dressing room demanding fried pickles made with love. The pickle rescue fails, Harriet's tomato sandwich succeeds, and when Vic introduces the hit live, he names Louis as its writer. Harriet learns her idol was a ventriloquist's dummy, and that fairness sometimes arrives step by step.

stories.situation: Harriet and her mom enter the Birdstravaganza photo contest hunting the ruby-crowned kinglet, her mom fishing for a museum donation from the imperious bird-watcher Iris Vanderyke. The two are too different in every habit, they bicker through the park, split up, and both fail alone.
stories.coping: Each realizes the other had the missing piece, Harriet's spy instincts, her mom's polite cocoa diplomacy, and they pool information and work the trail together. Harriet stands up to Iris when she insults her mom, and the day ends with no photo and no donation but an impossible fun time together, agreed on for next year.
stories.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis frames the contest; the script shows the molting line, the Belgium cocoa trap that softens Iris's crew, Harriet telling off Iris, the five-dollar check, and the too-different/split-up/pool-information arc. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Harriet really wants to win a photo competition, but it means teaming up with someone she doesn't see eye to eye with: her mom.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harriet and her mom team up for the Central Park Birdstravaganza, her mom courting donor Iris Vanderyke for the museum's molting diorama, Harriet planning to out-spy the whole avian society and beat Iris's professional crew. They are opposites in every habit, bicker, and split up, and alone they both get lost, wet, and birdless. Pooling information brings them to the kinglet together, and when Iris insults her mom, Harriet defends her at the cost of banishment. No photo, a five-dollar donation, and the real prize: a fun day together and a rematch next year.

stories.synopsis: Sport and Harriet think it is time to get rid of their beloved stuffies, but Marion's sneaky reporting changes their minds and the narrative.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Sixth grade pressure has Harriet jiggling her leg, and spying reveals her unshakeable friend Sport calms down the same way she does: hugging his stuffy, Doctor Bunny. Marion catches them with Eddie Spaghetti and Doctor Bunny on camera and threatens a newsletter exposé, so Harriet plans a Crybaby Bridge farewell for her toast-smelling duck. But neither friend can let go, a tugboat horn rules in the stuffies' favor, and instead of hiding they march into school and out them as stuffy huggers. One by one classmates introduce Gunther the Bear and friends, Marion's camera gets confiscated, and being a stuffy hugger becomes something to declare, not deny.

stories.situation: Harriet starts spying on the new Garcia family and their son Carlos, who vanishes every night at game-show time, and discovers Carlos has a map of her spy route with her name on it. Sure he is an international spy, then the Bodega Burglar, she steals his decoy keys, gets caught mid-theft, and runs for her life.
stories.coping: The chase ends on a rooftop where both spies finally talk instead of tail each other: Carlos was decoy-baiting the real burglar, and the Garcias and Harriet's friends have already caught the thief together. Harriet admits running away from each other less and talking more is how amazing friendships happen, and Carlos becomes the friend she wishes for.
stories.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis stops at discovering the counter-spy; the script carries the Bodega Burglar false lead, the penny-candy key theft, the rooftop showdown, and the decoy-keys reversal that makes Carlos a hero and a friend. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Harriet adds the Garcia family to her spy route...and discovers that someone is spying on her.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harriet adds the newly arrived Garcia family to her spy route and notices their son Carlos disappears every night at exactly game-show time. Every theory runs from international spy to Bodega Burglar, and when she lifts what look like his keys, Carlos chases her across midtown. On the rooftop the truth flips: the keys were decoy bait Carlos set for the real thief, the Garcias and Harriet's friends have already caught the burglar, and the two spies finally talk instead of tail each other. stories.situation: Harriet's beloved last baby tooth, General Mouthwashington, commander of her Revolutionary-War mouth games, needs to be extracted, and Harriet fights the order with stretching, second opinions, and skipped appointments, because losing the tooth feels like losing being little.
stories.coping: After a tomato sandwich turns painful, Harriet admits the fear instead of winning the argument, and Ole Golly tells her plainly that part of growing up is learning to let go. Harriet finds the courage to sit in the chair, donates the tooth to science, and keeps the general's story, since nothing is truly gone if its story lives on.

stories.synopsis: When Harriet loses her last and favorite baby tooth, she struggles with saying goodbye to her babyhood.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harriet's favorite last baby tooth, General Mouthwashington of her Revolutionary-War dental adventures, is boxed in by incoming adult teeth and scheduled for extraction. She tries stretching her mouth three inches, recruiting a second opinion from a dad with missing teeth, and flat-out skipping the appointment, until a tomato sandwich finally hurts. Ole Golly tells her the truth: growing up means learning to let go. Harriet rides out with courage, sends the general's body to science to keep up the good bite, and learns that nothing is truly gone if its story lives on. Her parents, meanwhile, decide their 12-year-old wedding cake was never really about the cake.

stories.synopsis: After Harriet makes an unexpected discovery, she comes up with a plan to right her wrongs.
stories.perStorySynopsis: On the night of the harvest moon, Harriet's notebook comes back to her doorstep, but her heart is not in it: she tells her parents she cannot be a writer if everything she writes hurts people. Ole Golly's letter sets her straight, writing is to put love in the world, not to use against your friends, and an apology is owed. stories.episodeTitle: It's My Party and I'll Spy If I Want To
stories.situation: The Robinsons are moving away, and Harriet has one last party to crack the story of the dullest couple on her spy route before they vanish. Disguised in a dress, she hunts them through an adult party full of casserole rivalries, comedians, and conga lines, and stumbles into the dreaded kids' room ruled by little kids.
stories.coping: When her suspect list flies loose, Harriet ends up teaming with Pinky Whitehead, the boy she never gave a chance, and the two win the charades game that finally makes the Robinsons laugh and play. Harriet never cracks the secret story, and decides the story she found instead, the first chapter of getting to know Pinky, is better.
stories.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis is the setup; the script shows the kids-room pip-squeak feeding frenzy, the casserole war, the charades partnership with Pinky, and the ending where the better story is Harriet's own new friendship. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: The Welsch family attends a neighborhood party where Harriet is determined to find out why the Robinsons are so boring.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The Robinsons, so boring they make belly button lint seem exciting, are moving away, and Harriet goes to a neighborhood party in her fiendish disguise (a dress) determined to find their true story before they escape. She survives the dreaded kids' room, narrates the adults like a nature documentary, and loses her secret-identity list. stories.situation: Benjamin's Captain Spin crash lands into Piper's book castle, and the apology does not rebuild it: she bans him from her room. Story time picks up the wreckage, because the Big Bad Wolf is about to blow down a pig house, and Piper interrupts to ask him nicely to stop.
stories.coping: Papa teaches the actual lever: character is not what you like, it is how you treat others. Rewrites that only change the wolf's hobbies just move the mess around, until Piper writes kindness in, and the frame story repairs itself when Captain Spin returns, changed, to help rebuild.
stories.notes: mixed age: fairy-tale slapstick plays 2-4 but the double lesson, banning a sibling versus rewriting a character, plays 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Piper tries to save the Three Little Pigs' omits the frame-story fight with Benjamin that the wolf tale is quietly solving. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Piper tries to save the Three Little Pigs from the Big Bad Wolf. When Terry Turtle hatches all alone, Piper and Papa help him find his way.
stories.perStorySynopsis: When Benjamin's spinning crashes Piper's book castle, her room closes to him, and bedtime story time becomes the negotiation table. Piper interrupts the Three Little Pigs to reform the Big Bad Wolf, and learns that swapping pizza for tuba for ballet only relocates the wreckage: character is how you treat others. Her final draft writes a helping wolf, and Captain Spin, take notes, comes back to help rebuild the castle he flattened.

stories.episodeTitle: Not So Bad Wolf / Chicken of the Sea
stories.situation: Terry Turtle hatches alone with one job, follow the moon to the ocean, and the beach supplies driftwood, dunes, and pirate crabs between him and it. Duckston keeps writing gave-up-and-ate-oatmeal endings, because the space between the puzzle bins has taught him lost things stay lost.
stories.coping: Piper keeps rewriting past every impossible, seaweed slingshot, coconut-shell glider, a lullaby played to pirates, and the story ends at Turtle Island with family. Back in the classroom, the impossible sticker is sitting exactly where creative thinking put it.
stories.notes: mixed age: pirate crabs play 2-4; the tug-of-war between a friend who says impossible and a story that keeps going, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Piper and Papa help him find his way' omits Duckston's surrender endings, the crew's escape-by-lullaby, and the sticker echo that closes the loop. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Piper tries to save the Three Little Pigs from the Big Bad Wolf. When Terry Turtle hatches all alone, Piper and Papa help him find his way.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Terry Turtle hatches alone on a beach, and every step toward the ocean grows an obstacle, driftwood, dunes, a one-way pirate crew. Duckston keeps writing endings where everyone gives up and eats oatmeal, and Piper keeps interrupting with creative ideas until the story delivers Terry to his family. Back in class, the sticker that fell into the forever-lost space turns out not to be lost after all.

stories.episodeTitle: The Elephant of Surprise / The Chicken and the Egg
stories.situation: Piper jumps into the Billy Goats Gruff and helpfully tells the troll the goats' whole plan, which ends the story on the spot. Mrs. Slothworth's lesson, every story has the element of surprise, gets taken literally, an elephant of surprise, and the rewrite has to win the meadow back with tricks the troll cannot predict.
stories.coping: Piper's second draft gives the troll nothing to expect: a fake long-way-around, coconut rattle, goats that faint, and a brand-new bridge built while he argues with a tummy growl. The troll hates surprises, which is exactly the point, and Theodore's magic trick closes the loop.
stories.notes: mixed age: fainting goats play 2-4; hearing that helping can spoil a story, and fixing the fix, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'outsmart the Bridge Troll' omits that Piper's first intervention is the problem and the elephant pun drives the whole structure. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Piper and the Three Billy Goats Gruff outsmart the Bridge Troll. The King's Knights help Piper solve a royal mystery.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Piper's helpful interruption tells the troll the goats' entire plan and ends the story early, her first rewrite that backfired. Papa introduces the element of surprise, via a literal elephant in Rapunzel's tower, and the rerun of the Billy Goats Gruff becomes a masterclass in misdirection, complete with fainted goats and a secretly built second bridge. The troll surrenders to a story he could not predict.

stories.episodeTitle: The Elephant of Surprise / The Chicken and the Egg
stories.situation: Piper's art project has become a paint-glitter-paper avalanche, and the harder she grabs, the worse it gets. Story time hands her Humpty Dumpty in pieces and a rhyme that says nobody could put him together again, with a king's glue locked behind an obstacle course of doom.
stories.coping: Papa offers the writer's tool, a story beat, one small thing that moves the story forward, and Piper stacks them: a snack break, a map, a quest, one more beat after every failure. Humpty gets glued, whole again, and the same beats un-do the art avalanche at home.
stories.notes: mixed age: the sandwich knight plays 2-4; a big overwhelming mess broken into next steps, in craft and in story, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'The King's Knights help Piper solve a royal mystery' is the other story; tags anchor on segment_title plus the script. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Piper and the Three Billy Goats Gruff outsmart the Bridge Troll. The King's Knights help Piper solve a royal mystery.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Piper's cleanup attempt is losing to her own art supplies, and Humpty Dumpty is losing to gravity, with a rhyme insisting he stays broken. Papa teaches story beats, one small step that moves things forward, and Piper beats her way through sandwiches, maps, quests, and an obstacle course of doom to the king's glue. Humpty ends up whole, and the same method tidies the bedroom that started it all.

stories.episodeTitle: Hercul-easy / The Lion, the Mouse and the Chicken
stories.situation: Piper interrupts Hercules' trials and clears every obstacle, boulder moved, wall scaled, maze opened, so the hero-in-training can just walk to his trophy. The urn story stops: no trophy, because nothing was in his way.
stories.coping: Papa names the missing piece, an obstacle, and Piper's next rewrite puts all the obstacles back, boulder, wall, runaway boulder, broken wheel. Hercules earns two trophies, and the classroom hoop gets raised on purpose, because easy was boring.
stories.notes: mixed age: the chariot chase plays 2-4; the idea that difficulty is not the enemy of the thing you want but the price of it, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'make Hercules' heroic journey easier' omits that the easy version fails, the obstacles get restored on purpose, and the Parthenon gets saved instead. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: In Greece, Piper attempts to make Hercules' heroic journey easier. A lion with a thorn in his paw resists help.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Piper does young Hercules the kindest possible sabotage, removing every obstacle between him and the hero's trophy, and the story refuses to end well. Papa explains that heroes are made by obstacles, not despite them, so the rewrite puts the boulder back, and a runaway boulder turns restoration into real heroics. Back at school, the basketball hoop goes back up: the game needs things in the way.

stories.segmentTitle: The Lion, the Mouse and the Chicken
stories.situation: Piper is at the doctor's office trying to rename herself out of a wing appointment, and the story supplies a lion with a thorn in his paw who refuses the mouse's help. Every game the lion tries with friends fails on the paw, and the thorn gets worse.
stories.coping: Piper's rewrite lets the lion be scared out loud and still say yes: might it hurt, yes a little, and we will count to three together. The thorn comes out, the games come back, and Piper walks into her own appointment asking Papa to count with her.
stories.notes: mixed age: patty-cake with a limp plays 2-4; fear of a short hurt versus a long one, and letting someone help, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a lion with a thorn in his paw resists help' omits that the whole segment is Piper's own doctor fear wearing a lion costume. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: In Greece, Piper attempts to make Hercules' heroic journey easier. A lion with a thorn in his paw resists help.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Piper is hiding from a doctor's appointment under three fake names when Papa reads The Lion and the Mouse, whose hero refuses the one thing that would fix him. The lion's games evaporate and his paw gets worse, and Piper's rewrite gives him permission to be scared and counted through it. The moral arrives on time: let someone help you, even if you are scared, and the sprained wing gets wrapped in three counts flat.

stories.episodeTitle: Where's the Party? / Chicken Out West
stories.situation: Piper interrupts Aladdin to spend a wish on the genie, who has granted everyone else's wishes and never had his own. The ice cream party keeps failing by location, desert heat, South Pole freeze, forest ants, even the moon, and the search for the perfect place starts burning the day.
stories.coping: The search ends by looking at what was already loved: the genie's own lamp, perfect temperature, zero ants, ping-pong included. Piper apologizes for the failed hunt, the party happens at home base, and the backyard kites find the same answer at the lake.
stories.notes: mixed age: the location-hopping gags play 2-4; the person who gives and gives getting a turn, and perfect being closer than far away, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'search for the perfect place' omits that the wish is for the genie, and that every exotic setting fails until the lamp wins. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Piper, Aladdin, and Genie search for the perfect place to host an ice cream party. Piper joins the Pony Express.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Piper interrupts Aladdin mid-wish to ask a better question, when does the genie get a wish, and his ice cream party becomes the plot. Desert, South Pole, forest, and moon each ruin the party in a new way, until the perfect setting turns out to be the lamp the genie never wanted to leave. The grateful wish lands, and the backyard kite problem solves itself the same way, by changing where, not what.

stories.episodeTitle: Where's the Party? / Chicken Out West
stories.situation: Miss Clara leaves the Penelope Pony story on a cliffhanger, mid-mountain, letter undelivered, and Piper has to wait a whole day. Writing the continuation means committing to what happens next, over a bear, a broken bridge, a runaway letter, and a final cliff of her own invention.
stories.coping: When Piper's own story reaches a cliff she cannot write past, Papa's questions, did they ask for help, did they build something, unstick the pen. The lasso climb delivers the birthday letter, and Duckston's top secret package keeps its own cliffhanger for the fun of it.
stories.notes: mixed age: the pony express romp plays 2-4; living inside suspense on purpose, and writing past the moment you do not know, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Piper joins the Pony Express' omits the cliffhanger lesson, the waiting-for-tomorrow stake, and that Piper's stuck moment mirrors Penelope's mountain. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Piper, Aladdin, and Genie search for the perfect place to host an ice cream party. Piper joins the Pony Express.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Miss Clara's Pony Express story stops exactly where it gets dangerous, and Piper has to survive the suspense overnight. She writes Penelope's rescue herself, skis, bear, lasso, and discovers writers hit cliffs too, until the right question turns the blank page into a climb. The letter arrives for the birthday sister, and Duckston's mystery package holds its suspense like a professional.

stories.episodeTitle: Disco Chickens / Little Red and the Little Red Chicken
stories.situation: Grandma and Grandpa each tell the story of the night they met, and the two versions contradict on the moose, the polar bear, and who was the best skater. Both insist theirs is one hundred percent right, and a first meeting has become an argument.
stories.coping: Piper's detective story refuses to pick a winner: she collects every point of view, DJ included, and writes one combined story where both chickens are right. The balloon explains the polar bear, the bump explains the meet-cute, and Benjamin's four-headed monster turns out to be golf clubs once he looks closer.
stories.notes: mixed age: the disco gags play 2-4; two people remembering the same event differently, and both being true, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Piper investigates how Grandma and Grandpa met' omits the contradictory-testimony structure and Benjamin's monster subplot that rhymes with it. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: At a disco roller rink, Piper investigates how Grandma and Grandpa met. Piper tries to warn Little Red Riding Hood about the wolf.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Grandma and Grandpa remember meeting at the disco roller rink, and their memories disagree, best skater, headstand moose, spinning polar bear. Piper writes a detective story that interviews the whole rink and discovers the fix is not picking a winner but weaving every point of view into one story. Benjamin, meanwhile, meets the basement's four-headed monster and finds golf clubs, both mysteries solved by a change of view.

stories.segmentTitle: Little Red and the Little Red Chicken
stories.situation: Theodore forgot the photo of the flower he grew for show-and-tell, and every crayon fails to match Zinnie's exact purple, so he wants to quit. In the story, Piper cannot finish her warning because there is nothing to compare the wolf to, as bad as a what.
stories.coping: Mrs. Slothworth hands them the missing tool, the simile, and it does double duty: Little Red gets her warning in time, grandma returns from go-karting in Bolivia to evict the house-sitting wolf, and Theodore finds Zinnie's purple in grape jelly. Describing the thing unlocks both stories.
stories.notes: mixed age: the freezing-out-the-wolf plays 2-4; vocabulary as rescue equipment, when you cannot say what you mean, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Piper tries to warn Little Red Riding Hood' omits the stuck-in-the-middle-of-a-simile beat and the classroom mirror in Theodore's purple problem. confidence high.

Meanwhile Theodore cannot show-and-tell the flower he grew because no crayon matches Zinnie's purple. One lesson, the simile, saves both stories, complete with a South-Pole-cold elephant, a house-sitting wolf, and grape jelly.

stories.episodeTitle: Dawn of Wonder Chicken / The Chicken Who Cried Wolf
stories.situation: The board game stalls without its Mer-Rooster piece, and Piper's homemade Wonder Chicken story stalls for the same reason in reverse: a hero with no past. Every villain trap defeats her, quack-tanium lasers, darkened labs, headphone monsters, because nothing in her history gives her a tool for any of it.
stories.coping: Grandma teaches the fix, a backstory, everything from a character's past that makes them who they are. A lightning-struck weather book, computer practice, a pet monster, and a boyhood friend named Quackles turn out to be the whole solution, and even the villain gets grounded by his mom.
stories.notes: mixed age: the potato slapstick plays 2-4; the writing lesson that a character's past explains her powers, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Piper transforms into Wonder Chicken' omits that the episode is a writing workshop in disguise, and that the villain's defeat is a revelation, not a fight. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Piper transforms into Wonder Chicken to save Chickenopolis. After a shepherd boy cries wolf, Piper asks him about his motivation.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Wonder Chicken faces a quack-tanium laser grid with no tools, because Piper wrote her a hero with no history. Grandma supplies the writer's term, backstory, and each new memory, a thunder-cluck book, library computer skills, a pet monster, a childhood friend, becomes a way through. Dr. Von Duck falls not to a punch but to being recognized, and a missing Mer-Rooster gets a backstory that beats the real toy.

stories.episodeTitle: Dawn of Wonder Chicken / The Chicken Who Cried Wolf
stories.situation: Theodore fakes injuries, twice, and nobody believes him, right before story time casts a boy who cries wolf twice and loses his sheep. Piper interviews her way to the motivations under both tricks: the boy wanted an audience that really listened, and the wolf wanted company on his birthday.
stories.coping: The rewrite swaps punishment for understanding: the boy gets his audience, the wolf gets a sheep-over party with the whole village, and afterward Theodore tells the truth himself, he was hurting in here, and needed some extra attention. He gets the hug, not a lecture.
stories.notes: mixed age: the party reveal plays 2-4; attention-seeking as a feeling with a reason, said out loud and met with a hug, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a shepherd boy cries wolf' omits the motivation interviews, the wolf's lonely birthday, and Theodore's real confession afterward. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Piper transforms into Wonder Chicken to save Chickenopolis. After a shepherd boy cries wolf, Piper asks him about his motivation.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Theodore's fake injuries are followed by a story about a boy whose false wolf calls cost him his sheep, and Piper rewrites for motive instead of punishment: the boy wanted listeners, and the wolf stole sheep to fill a lonely birthday. The village ends up at a party, the boy sings for a real audience, and Theodore, having watched the whole thing, tells his own truth and gets a hug for it.

stories.episodeTitle: Arizona Chickenstone and the Temple of the Troll / The Chicken and the Beanstalk
stories.segmentTitle: Arizona Chickenstone and the Temple of the Troll
stories.situation: Theodore's journal says to take the path with the tree and the big rock, but every path has both, and the creek is lost until details return. In the story, Piper's adventure starts as a list of trusty gear and no pictures, quicksand included.
stories.coping: Papa's writing tool is vivid detail, enough description to picture it, and each dose does real work: troll footprints pick the path, vines escape the quicksand, a different brick opens a secret passage, stalactites hold the rope. Back on the trail, a big round green rock with moss finds the creek.
stories.notes: mixed age: the giant orange of doom plays 2-4; description as a survival tool for stories and for trails, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'rescues an artifact from a hidden jungle temple' omits the lost-creek frame and that every escape is powered by a writing lesson. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: As a world explorer, Piper rescues an artifact from a hidden jungle temple. Piper reimagines Jack and the Beanstalk from the giant's perspective.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Theodore's explorer journal points to a tree and a big rock, which describes every path in the woods, so Papa reads an explorer story where vivid detail saves the day. Piper writes Arizona Chickenstone through quicksand, troll traps, and a collapsing temple using nothing but well-chosen specifics, then borrows the technique to find a mossy rock. The creek appears, exactly where the details said.

stories.episodeTitle: Arizona Chickenstone and the Temple of the Troll / The Chicken and the Beanstalk
stories.situation: Benjamin's gloppy paint project looks like a mess, and Jack's harp theft looks like a happy ending, until Piper asks the second question. From the giant's side, the beanstalk brought a ghost, a theft, and a stolen practice partner with a library show coming up.
stories.coping: Piper writes the story again from the giant's eyes, Jack hears what the harp really meant and returns it with an apology, and everyone's ending gets rewritten together, music in the woods, weekly. Then Mom asks Benjamin's perspective, and the gloppy paint becomes a gift Emilo can feel.
stories.notes: mixed age: the giant's haunted-house comedy plays 2-4; perspective-taking as a habit, with a blind friend who experiences art by touch, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'reimagines Jack and the Beanstalk from the giant's perspective' omits Emilo, the frame-story apology, and the shared ending. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: As a world explorer, Piper rescues an artifact from a hidden jungle temple. Piper reimagines Jack and the Beanstalk from the giant's perspective.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Jack's beanstalk caper ends happily for Jack, and Piper notices someone did not get a happy ending: the giant whose harp disappeared. Rewriting the story from her point of view turns a victory into an apology, and a new ending where the music belongs to everyone, including Jack's mom. Mom applies the same lesson at home and learns Benjamin's gloppy mess is a painting made to be touched.

stories.situation: Duckston's moon costume piece is missing, Benjamin refuses his own costume because it is not spooky enough, and Piper's Halloween story has a monster that will not scare anyone: she wrote spooky and described nothing.
stories.coping: Papa coaches Piper through the five senses, and the monster gets a look, a growl, slimy claws, and old-wet-laundry smell until the room is properly spooked. The same tool finds the moon, round, white, string attached, squishy, light as air, a balloon, up.
stories.notes: mixed age: the spook-level gags play 2-4; saying spooky is not showing spooky, and senses as search equipment, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Piper writes a spooky monster story' omits the five-sense rewrite, the missing balloon moon, and Benjamin's costume rescue. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: On Halloween, Piper writes a spooky monster story. Piper helps the Sorcerer's Apprentice outsmart a four-headed dragon.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Piper's Halloween monster is a failure by the villagers' reviews, because she wrote the word spooky instead of building one. Sense by sense, Papa's story-time workshop makes it real, and the same describing trick solves Duckston's missing moon, which turns out to be a balloon floating overhead. Trick-or-treating finally launches, costumes complete.

stories.situation: The apprentice tries one spell to clean up, breaks the cleanup, and breaks it again, then learns the staff's rule the hard way: the same magic word cannot be used twice in one day. Fast is spent, big is spent, and four dragon heads are guarding the slippers.
stories.coping: Piper supplies the loophole, a synonym, another word that means the same thing, and the apprentice runs the ladder: swift, leap, immense, then kind, friendly, and pleasant, one per head. The slippers go home, the dragon gets warm socks, and the sorcerer hands over a promotion.
stories.notes: mixed age: the four-headed politeness offensive plays 2-4; running out of words for what you need, and growing your vocabulary instead, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'helps the Sorcerer's Apprentice outsmart a four-headed dragon' omits the magic-word rule and that synonyms are the weapon. confidence high.

stories.perStorySynopsis: A sorcerer's apprentice with one magic word per day is in trouble, because he already said fast and big. Piper interrupts with the fix: synonyms, swift and leap and immense, then a different nice-adjacent word for each of four dragon heads. The slippers come home carried by newly polite dragons, and the apprentice earns a thesaurus of his own.

stories.situation: Ebenezer Wolf cancels every holiday at once and confiscates the presents, decorations, and eggnog, because he only ever gets socks and only sees fuss. Tiny Pig keeps making his yearly snowflake for the wolf anyway, the one delivery the wolf never lets him make.
stories.coping: Piper picks the theme before the plot, giving, and writes three ghosts of giving, past, present, and future, to show the wolf what he already knows: the one time he gave mittens away, it felt great. He uncancels the holidays, gives Tiny Pig scissors and paper, and receives the best snowflake of his life.
stories.notes: special episode: holiday special with the whole class party frame. mixed age: the ghost gags play 2-4; the mechanics of a change of heart, theme first, ghosts as evidence, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'teams up with the Three Little Pigs to save the season' omits the ghost structure, Tiny Pig's snowflake thread, and the kids' own written gifts at the party. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: When Ebenezer Wolf decides to cancel the holidays, Piper teams up with the Three Little Pigs to save the season. The chicken family throws a holiday party.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Ebenezer Wolf cancels the entire holiday season and confiscates the town's joy, and Piper's rewrite gives him the traditional three ghosts with a theme attached: giving. stories.episodeTitle: Captain Claw's Clawsome Quest / Cinderella's Story
stories.situation: CJ is too fast for anyone to want to race her, and Captain Claw is too good for anyone to want to compete, so the greatest pirate on the seven seas quits for pancakes. Piper writes her a foil, Captain Glitterbeard, mean where she is kind, cowardly where she is brave.

stories.coping: Mrs. Slothworth names the tool, sequence, the order things happen in, and the kids sort the pages, chores, magic, carriage, ball, until the story works. The missing ending gets written new, a fairy god-chicken teaches the Pumpkin Slide step by step, and the clapping game clicks.

stories.episodeTitle: Funky Chicken / Hansel & Gretel and the Chicken
stories.situation: Papa's friend brings hip-hop to story time, and Piper meets a classic tale that is somebody else's rhythm: how do you rewrite a story that everyone already knows, so it is still the story and still yours.
stories.coping: The hip-hop frame shows the way, same story, new flow: beats for the huffing, rhymes for the huff-and-puff, and a fairy tale that finds its own groove. Piper's version keeps every story bone and changes every step.
stories.notes: vibe call: hip-hop episode, high energy; noted for calibration. mixed age: the beat-based retelling plays 2-4 as sound and motion; remixing something classic so it becomes yours, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Piper rewrites a time-honored tale to make it her own' omits the hip-hop frame entirely. confidence high.

stories.coping: Papa names tone, what a writer does to create a feeling, and Piper tunes it piece by piece: a calm line for Gretel, cartwheels instead of walking, a witch whose scary party becomes a tea dance party. Benjamin tries the technique out loud on his sister, pretty please with strawberries on top, and the truck appears.
stories.notes: mixed age: the witch's glow-up plays 2-4; naming the tone of a story and of an ask, then adjusting both, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Piper rewrites a time-honored tale' omits the tone lesson, the scared frame, and the ask-differently resolution. confidence high.
