stories.episodeTitle: Save the Stalk! / Why Did the Chicken Cross the Road?
stories.situation: The knights arrive to chop the beanstalk for a carriage parking lot, on royal orders, and the king has a garden's worth of reasons not to listen. Persuasion attempt one, ladybugs, bounces off, and the knights' lances are already out.
stories.coping: Papa teaches persuasive writing, a goal plus reasons that matter to the listener: ladybugs for the king's nature side, giant pinecones for his crafts side, mushrooms for the troll's stomach. Each audience gets its own reason, the decree flips, and at home the kids write their own persuasive case to stay up and smell the jasmine.
stories.notes: mixed age: the googly-eyed pinecone plays 2-4; changing a mind by arguing the other person's reasons instead of your own, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Grandpa encourages Piper to help a struggling storybook character' omits the three-audience persuasion ladder and the bedtime-frame payoff. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Grandpa encourages Piper to help a struggling storybook character. A friendly lion looks to improve his comedy act.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The king's knights are ordered to fell the beanstalk for a carriage lot, and Piper saves it with persuasive writing, goal first, then a reason shaped for each listener: ladybugs for the king, giant craft pinecones, mushrooms for a hungry bridge troll. Every persuasion lands except the one aimed at a cowless Mysterious Dude, who gives the last magic bean for free because the reasons were good. The kids then write their own persuasive case to stay up and smell the night-blooming jasmine, and win.

stories.coping: Grandpa and Piper build the show from types of comedy: jokes, physical comedy, and surprise comedy, taught by the Elephant of Surprise. The birthday show mixes all three, and the answer to the old joke turns out to be a story with a funny ending.

stories.episodeTitle: Mary Had a Little Chicken / The Princess, the Chicken, and the Pea
stories.situation: Movie night dies in a neighborhood blackout, and a nursery rhyme is the only screen available. Piper retells Mary Had a Little Lamb across three genres, science fiction, Western, and action, while Mary herself keeps not looking before she leaps: a meteor, outlaws, a bubble monster.
stories.coping: Grandma and Grandpa supply the tool, genre, the style a story is in, and each swap brings its own gear: rocket suits, a ketchup shootout, a bubble emergency. The lesson underneath never changes, look before you leap, and the lights come back on mid-genre.
stories.notes: mixed age: the bubble monster plays 2-4; the same story told three ways, and what a genre actually changes, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'fun genre twists on a familiar favorite' omits the blackout frame, the three-genre run, and the repeated look-before-you-leap spine. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Piper puts fun genre twists on a familiar favorite. When a royal athlete can't fall asleep, Piper hunts the cause.

Each genre change swaps the setting and keeps the lesson: Mary, look before you leap. Lights, and story night, are restored by the final genre.

stories.situation: Princess Emerald cannot sleep before her pole vault tournament, and every fix causes a new problem: a cat invited in, a dinner bell rung quietly, knights awake and hungry, a spooked horse, a windmill, a blanketless dragon. The kingdom is wide awake because Piper keeps solving one link at a time.
stories.coping: Papa teaches cause and effect, why something happens and what happened, then how to think backwards from the effect you want. One dragon fireball relights the lantern, the horse stops, the wind dies, the blanket returns, the knights get tomatoes, and the kingdom sleeps in one linked chain.
stories.notes: mixed age: the sleepy chain reaction plays 2-4; tracing an effect back to its cause, and fixing the first link instead of the last, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a royal athlete can't fall asleep, Piper hunts the cause' omits the cascade of Piper-caused side effects and the backwards-thinking fix. confidence high.

The princess sleeps, vaults, and wins, and a stick fort gets rebuilt by the same logic.

stories.segmentTitle: The Magnificent Magician of the Mailbox
stories.situation: Three writers want one driveway story about three different things, waffles, robots, magic, and the chalk is not moving. When they do collaborate, each wish-giver in the story turns out to already have the thing they were searching for, which they only notice by comparing notes.
stories.coping: Papa breaks collaboration into brainstorm, then choose together: a rain cloud, a robot, and a koala share one tub and one quest. When the magician has no snack, Duckston's waffle idea finally gets its moment, and the wishes are already granted by the journey itself.
stories.notes: mixed age: the purple brick path plays 2-4; brainstorming as a group skill where every idea waits for its turn, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'work together on an illustrated story' omits the brainstorm mechanics and the wishes-already-came-true twist. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Theodore, Duckston, and Piper work together on an illustrated story. Mrs. Slothworth teaches a lesson about collaboration.

When the Magician of the Mailbox cannot grant wishes on an empty stomach, the leftover waffle idea saves the day. The magician's real magic is the reveal: every wish already came true somewhere on the Purple Brick Path.

stories.situation: The King's knights have never ridden a roller coaster, let alone built one, and Piper's own expertise turns out to be a ride on one, not blueprints. The carnival is tonight, and the royal thing to do is cancel it.
stories.coping: Piper learns research as a real skill with four doors: read about it, ask an expert, run an experiment, experience it yourself. The carnival opens on a working coaster, and the class field trip is the truest research of all.

stories.episodeTitle: Wonder Chicken Returns / Professor Goose Visits
stories.situation: Wonder Chicken befriends her supervillain over ice cream, and the friendship becomes the problem: every game Von Duck and Mega Potato play splashes, freezes, or wrecks the city, and stopping them wrecks the friendship. Tag without a tag, an unspoken hurt, is humming underneath in the yard.
stories.coping: The Coop of Wisdom sorts three kinds of conflict, story, internal, and with the environment, and the resolution Piper writes is a feelings conversation: you are wrecking the city for everyone who lives here. The friends find a potato-sized compromise, and CJ finds her voice about tag.
stories.notes: mixed age: the belly-flop plot plays 2-4; naming what you feel and saying it to a friend, plus the harder truth that you can like someone and still need them to stop, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Grandma teaches a valuable lesson' omits the friendship-with-a-villain bind and the CJ tag subplot. confidence high.

stories.coping: Papa supplies the writer's toolkit in order: fold the paper into a book, know your audience, make a word web, then write the ending part last. A meteor shower and a picnic-stealing space monster turn out to be one story, and everyone at the picnic is a friend Piper wrote in.

Jinja engineers her way there on snack pails, Harvey bounces in on a borrowed ball, and the tie breaks when an ice cream flies: Harvey saves it, loses the race, and declares Jinja the winner on the spot. She trades her prize cone for the right to hand him the first one, ketchup and dog treats, his favorites.

stories.situation: Harvey and Robin get zapped to Lumington, a town with one tree, one wall, a toast truck, and no Thankful Day, while the festival back home goes on without them. Lucy drives the only bus and Leonard has never once been thanked for anything.
stories.coping: Harvey does what he does anywhere: thanks the bench out loud, and the town starts to glow. The friends turn a missed festival into a brand new one, Lumington's own, with rock races, a Thankful Bus for a tree, and two hosts who learned the feeling themselves.
stories.notes: mixed age: the tour-of-nothing comedy plays 2-4; gratitude as a skill you can learn anywhere, and the friends who follow your glow, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'find ways to be grateful for the unexpected' is the spine; the script adds the zapped-by-invention setup, Lucy's first thank you ever, and that the Sagoville crew finds them by following the glow. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: When an invention mishap sends Harvey and Robin far from Sagoville, they find ways to be grateful for the unexpected. Alan tests a new invention.
stories.perStorySynopsis: A here-to-there-inator sends Harvey and Robin nowhere near the top of the Thankful Tree and somewhere named Lumington, while the festival they love happens without them. What the plainer town in the world needs, it turns out, is exactly what Harvey carries: a thank you said out loud, to a bench, that makes Lucy glow. The tour becomes a lesson, the bus becomes a Thankful Tree, and when their friends finally find them, the best Thankful Day ever happens right where they were lost.

stories.situation: Harvey's beloved lunch box splits at the seams, and instead of a sad goodbye he reopens it as a treasure box where every friend picks a prize. Then the treasures come out sideways: a sock, cracked spoons, wrapping paper, and nobody can see what any of it is worth.
stories.coping: Each doubt gets answered with a whole adventure story that proves the treasure: a sock parachute in space, cowgirl Jinja's spoons of glory, Sir Robin's wrapping-paper shield. The box is empty by the end, which is the good part, and the friends refill it for Harvey with an egg carton that is definitely a submarine.
stories.notes: mixed age: the story-within-story games play 2-4; finding worth in what looks like trash, and proving value by using it, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'finds new life as a treasure box' omits the doubt-from-friends beat and the story-as-proof structure that carries the whole segment. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: An old lunch box finds new life when Harvey transforms it into a treasure box full of unique items. Harvey discovers a hidden talent.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harvey's split lunch box becomes a treasure box, and the treasure is junk until the stories start: a sock that saves two space rangers, cracked spoons that herd calves, wrapping paper that becomes a knight's shield, crown, and key. One by one the friends stop seeing trash and start seeing what a thing can do, and the empty box ends up more valuable full of friends' refills than it ever was full of lunch.

stories.situation: The friends have fallen asleep before the New Year's bell every single year, and this year Harvey refuses again. Steve the new firefly has never granted a wish, the hunt for ten horns and nine fancy things runs out of stars, and the shooting star slips away at the last second.
stories.coping: Robin says it first: the wish failed, and the night is still really thankful-worthy, they met a firefly, had pizza, made their own surprises. Then the bell rings while everyone is awake anyway, and the year's last surprise is theirs without any magic at all.
stories.notes: mixed age: the countdown hunt plays 2-4; trying hard for a thing that does not come, and finding the night was still enough, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a firefly named Steve helps grant a New Year's wish' omits that the wish technically fails, and that the kids see the bell awake because the hunt kept them up. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: When a firefly named Steve helps grant a New Year's wish, the gang goes on a scavenger hunt. The friends celebrate New Year's Eve with a scavenger hunt.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Every New Year's Eve ends the same way in Sagoville, asleep before the bell, so Harvey enlists Steve, a firefly brand new to wish granting, and a twelve-item scavenger hunt to keep everyone awake. The hunt succeeds beautifully right up until it does not, the shooting star is lost, and the wish dies with it. The friends choose thankfulness over disappointment, and the surprise they have missed every year arrives while they are still up, singing about their own.

stories.situation: Jinja's new dance is phenomenal and Harvey keeps flopping at it: his tail wags him over, his ears blind him, his legs will not jump a flip. Everyone else can do it, even Jack, and Harvey quits on the spot, no, I do not.
stories.coping: Fins refuses to say keep trying and tells the truth instead: your body moves in a different way, everybody's does. Harvey goes back and does not master Jinja's dance, he makes his own, a Harvey dance with the ears and tail built in, and it is phenomenal.
stories.notes: mixed age: the flop comedy plays 2-4; the difference between keep trying and find your own way is the lesson for kids who cannot do the thing everyone else can. script_vs_synopsis: 'tries to find his own groove' hides the quit-then-return arc and Fins' reframe that the problem was never effort. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: After struggling to learn Jinja's dance, Harvey tries to find his own groove. Jinja inspires Harvey to keep trying new things.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harvey wants to do Jinja's phenomenal new dance, and his body keeps voting no: tail knocks him down, ears cover his eyes, flips stay out of reach. A retreat to the pond ends not with try harder but with something truer, from a fish who gets around on his tail, that everybody moves in different ways. Harvey returns with a dance that is nobody's but his, tail and ears and all, and the whole town dances along.

stories.situation: Jinja builds a cozy fort for one, built for one me, and Harvey builds his own out of treats. It is cozy, and delicious, and something does not feel right: the quiet inside a fort built for one is bigger than the fort.
stories.coping: Harvey cannot name it at first, then says it anyway, that something does not feel right, and Jinja comes over with yarn. One friend becomes every friend, and when the forts all crash together the pieces become one big fort, built for everybody.
stories.notes: mixed age: fort building and silly faces play 2-4; the discovery that cozy-for-one is lonelier than it sounds lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Harvey tries to find his own groove' is the other story; this one's spine is the lonely fort that ends up big enough for everyone. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: After struggling to learn Jinja's dance, Harvey tries to find his own groove. Jinja inspires Harvey to keep trying new things.

He admits something does not feel right, and the visitors keep arriving until a ruckus collapses every fort in Sagoville into one heap of parts. Harvey sees the pile and sees an answer, the coziest fort ever, big enough for all of them.

stories.episodeTitle: Piece of Cake / X Marks the Spot
stories.situation: Remy's winter party has no cake, so his friends volunteer to bake one, and Remy gives the exact spec: vanilla, white frosting, white sprinkles, big. Harvey remembers the big part and adds pinch after pinch of growing powder, and the perfect cake keeps growing out of the kitchen, across the floor, and out of reach of the party.
stories.coping: Harvey says it himself before anyone else can, I added a lot, and owns the mistake out loud to Remy. The fix is a flip: they cannot bring the cake to the party, so the whole conga line brings the party to the cake.
stories.notes: mixed age: the runaway-cake musical plays 2-4; a mistake made with good intentions, said out loud and fixed sideways, is the tag lesson for making mistakes. script_vs_synopsis: 'a small mistake leads to a big problem' is the spine; the script adds that Remy's own instructions fed the mistake, and that his thank you comes before he has even seen the cake. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: As Harvey and Jinja bake a cake for Remy, a small mistake leads to a big problem. Harvey and Robin play in a new fort.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Remy's winter party needs one thing, and the bakery has none, so Harvey and Jinja bake from his exact wish list. Then Harvey adds a teensy bit more growing powder, then a pinch for every friend on the guest list, and the cake outgrows the house while the party waits. He tells Remy the truth, the conga line reroutes to Harvey's kitchen, and the biggest, sparkliest, most wonderfully wintry cake in Sagoville serves everyone one super tasty piece.

stories.episodeTitle: Piece of Cake / X Marks the Spot
stories.situation: Jack turns up at the beach in full pirate kit on a treasure quest, digs up a real chest, and finds it empty. A pirate without treasure is no pirate at all, so the hat, jacket, beard, eye patch, and compass come off piece by piece, and even pirate underwear.
stories.coping: Harvey names the heartbreak out loud, that opening the empty chest broke his heart, and the friends answer by building Jack a brand new quest: a homemade map, a chest buried by pirates they know, and treasure inside this time. The shell and the fruit basket prove he was a pirate all along.
stories.notes: mixed age: the dig and the songs play 2-4; a friend's dream deflating, and rebuilding it yourself for them, is the 5-7 carry. script_vs_synopsis: 'Harvey and Robin play in a new fort' is a different story entirely, the catalog synopsis pairs to the other half; tags are anchored on segment_title and the script. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: As Harvey and Jinja bake a cake for Remy, a small mistake leads to a big problem. Harvey and Robin play in a new fort.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Jack arrives a pirate and leaves the beach undressed, hat, jacket, beard, and dignity stripped off layer by layer after an empty treasure chest. Harvey and the crew will not let the dream die in a hole: they draw their own map, recruit Umi to bury a chest, and send Jack on one more X-marked adventure made of friends. What he digs up is real this time, and so is the pirate he stayed.

stories.situation: Alan's spaceship house is a wonder of unlabeled buttons, and Alan cannot remember what any of them do. Harvey and Jack launch a helpful project, push a button, put a sticky picture on, until one push starts the whole ship shaking and another launches them into outer space with no way home.
stories.coping: The panic has a method: they name the problem, hunt the seat eject button in a pond, and ring Alan's doorbell, in space, to confess. Alan is delighted rather than upset, the labeling gets finished with the sticky picture maker, and the last untried button turns out to be the Sagoville button.
stories.notes: mixed age: the space romp plays 2-4; helpfulness that outruns permission, and the apology that fixes it, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'end up on an adventure through space' omits that the trip starts as a labeling project for a forgetful friend and ends in a confession at a space doorbell. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: When Harvey and Jack visit Alan's house, they end up on an adventure through space. Harvey joins a magical quest.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Alan's buttons baffle even Alan, so Harvey and Jack volunteer to test every single one and label it with a sticky picture. The project works beautifully until one button shakes the ship and another fires them past planets with no Sagoville button in sight. A soaked seat-eject recovery, a sheepish doorbell confession, and one more untried button later, everyone is home, the labels are on, and the spaceship crew shares alien cereal.

stories.situation: Fins has trained all season for his biggest-ever dive off the biggest-ever waterfall, and every pinecone family, salamander, and sparkle spring on the trail pulls Harvey's eyes sideways. The detours cost them the one cable car, and the dive Fins prepared for does not happen.
stories.coping: Fins says the truth without meanness, we missed it, then lets Harvey turn the day around: the acorn Nutmeg dropped is worth chasing. The squirrel chase they almost skipped becomes the best part, and Nutmeg's flying squirrel plane still gets Fins to his dive.
stories.notes: mixed age: the squirrel chase plays 2-4; two friends with different paces meeting in the middle, and a missed big moment being survived, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Harvey joins a magical quest' is the other story's line; tags anchor on segment_title plus the script. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: When Harvey and Jack visit Alan's house, they end up on an adventure through space. Harvey joins a magical quest.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Fins is focused and Harvey is a firehose of wonder, and their walk to the biggest-ever dive is a tug of war between the two. Every detour Harvey loves costs time, and the missed cable car costs Fins his dive, a quiet, honest disappointment. Then one dropped acorn turns the day: the chase to return it is the adventure neither planned, and a flying squirrel named Nutmeg delivers them both to the waterfall after all.

stories.episodeTitle: Home with Herb / Follow That Squeak
stories.situation: Alan asks Harvey to plant-sit Herb, one very important instruction forgotten on the way out the door. Herb looks sad, and Harvey pulls out everything that makes Harvey happy, squeaky toys, the playground, the merry-go-round, and Herb stays sad through all of it.
stories.coping: Harvey refuses to fake it: sorry Herb, I really wanted to take good care of you, but I just do not know how. The friends consult Jinja's plant books and try dirt, sun, and water first, and the answer arrives by accident, Herb lights up when Harvey picks him up.
stories.notes: mixed age: playground musical numbers play 2-4; doing your best for someone in your care and asking what they actually need, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Alan asks Harvey to care for his plant' omits the whole wrong-playground-right-plant arc and the forgotten instruction, which Alan remembers at the end: Herb likes to be held. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Alan asks Harvey to care for his plant, Herb. Harvey loses his beloved ball and travels around Sagoville chasing its squeak.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harvey takes plant-sitting seriously, and Herb will not cheer up no matter how much fun the playground has to offer. The friends research like pros, dirt parties, beach towels for sunshine, a rain dance, and the plant stays droopy, until Harvey admits he does not know how to care for Herb at all. The answer was in Harvey's arms the whole time, and Alan returns to build an Herb Holder so the holding can be official.

stories.coping: Harvey says the hard sentence, I think my ball is gone forever, and keeps going anyway. The friends build the rescue out of what everyone brought, a tricycle wheel, knitting needles, and Larry's missing poster, and Jack's eyes find the ball up Harvey's own tree.
stories.notes: mixed age: the squeak chase plays 2-4; persisting after grief says quit, with the whole town's help, is the tag lesson for losing something precious. script_vs_synopsis: 'travels around Sagoville chasing its squeak' is right; the script adds the chain of friendly false squeaks and the team-built ball rescue machine. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Alan asks Harvey to care for his plant, Herb. Harvey loses his beloved ball and travels around Sagoville chasing its squeak.

The search turns into a town-wide musical, everyone Harvey meets squeaks for a living, and hope thins out until Harvey says the words, gone forever. Then Jack spots orange and stripy in the tree, and a rescue machine cobbled from a trike wheel, knitting needles, and pure friendship brings the very best, most favorite ball home.

stories.episodeTitle: Gary's New Horn / Harvey Gets the Scoop
stories.situation: Gary's horn falls off, and the road to the Horn Fairy runs into a wall, a grumpy bridge-builder, and a lost butterfly named Tonk. Gary can no longer make rainbows, the thing his old horn was for, and watches the quest need exactly what he feels he has lost.
stories.coping: Gary keeps offering the horn he thinks is worthless, an ear-scratcher, a telescope, a salon for Hildi's hair, and grumpy feelings get chased away one helper at a time. At the fairy's door the truth comes out: the old horn was not done bringing happiness, and the new horn it earns makes the biggest rainbow of his life.
stories.notes: mixed age: the rainbow salon and horn ball play 2-4; losing the thing that made you special, and finding you still are, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a magical quest to meet the Horn Fairy' omits that the whole quest is powered by the horn Gary believes is broken. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Harvey joins Gary on a magical quest to meet the Horn Fairy. Dennis leaves Harvey in charge of his ice-cream truck.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Gary's beloved horn falls off, and the only cure is a quest to the Horn Fairy with the old horn in hand. Every obstacle on the way needs something Gary cannot do anymore, rainbows, until he discovers what a horn without rainbows can do: scratch an unreachable itch, find lost butterflies, curl a grump's hair, win at horn ball. The fairy takes the old horn with full honors, and the magnificent new one that replaces it spends its first minute making the biggest rainbow Gary has ever made.

stories.situation: Dennis closes the ice-cream truck to help at the pizza restaurant and hands Harvey the scoop, the steps, and a flavor map that defies memory. The customers keep coming with orders like pancake ice cream, seven brumble berries, fifteen sprinkles, and every order comes back wrong.
stories.coping: Harvey keeps saying the true thing under the chaos, being an ice-cream scooper is really hard, and lets Jinja's drawings help even after the drawings fail. The wrong orders become the Harvey Surprise, the most delicious creation his customers have ever tasted.
stories.notes: emoji note: replaced a non-emoji token with standard set. mixed age: flavor comedy plays 2-4; drowning in a job that looked easy, and letting mistakes become the specialty, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Dennis leaves Harvey in charge' omits Remy's impossible order, the failed picture menus, and that the signature sundae is invented by accident. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Harvey joins Gary on a magical quest to meet the Horn Fairy. Dennis leaves Harvey in charge of his ice-cream truck.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harvey's dream job comes with three easy steps and one impossible memory: freezer five has cheese, freezer six has toothpaste and lime, and there is no freezer two. The orders pile up wrong, the picture menus do not save him, and Harvey admits scooping is really hard. Then the mistakes start tasting delicious, the Harvey Surprise goes on the menu by accident, and Dennis comes back to a truck full of happy customers.

stories.situation: A perfect block tower crashes the second their backs turn, and a blue hair in the photo turns the cleanup into a manhunt. The trail of messes gets bigger, Jinja's library, Robin's toy bath, paint and eggs, until the blue mess-maker is cornered.
stories.coping: Blueberry Monster gets asked why instead of yelled at, and the why is simple: her hair is so long it covers her eyes, and she cannot see a thing she knocks over. The friends get her a haircut, hand back a town already tidied, and rebuild the tower together with their mystery guest.
stories.notes: mixed age: the chase numbers play 2-4; the lesson that a culprit is usually a problem you have not asked about yet, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'ready to find some answers' hides that the mess-maker is a nearsighted monster mid-haircut-quest, and that the kids had already cleaned most of her messes for her. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Someone is making messes around Sagoville, and Harvey and Jack are ready to find some answers! Blueberry Monster makes her debut.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The tallest block tower ever falls with no one near it, and a blue hair in the snapshot makes it a case. Harvey and Jack chase the mess across Sagoville, one toppled library and one saved rubber ducky later, and find Blueberry Monster, big, blue, and blindly bumping into everything because her hair hangs over her eyes. One haircut at Hugbot's later, the messes are explained, mostly cleaned by the friends themselves, and the tower goes back up taller with the mess-maker on the team.

stories.situation: Harvey is too muddy to play tag, basketball, or tea party, and every friend offers the same deal, a bath first. He shops for a friend who does not mind the mud, comes up empty, and declares he will stay by himself, forever, because he does not want the fix everyone is offering.
stories.coping: Robin does the thing Harvey cannot, helps him get clean, and the crew turns the bath he refused into a playtime bath party with a waterslide and supersized bubbles. He plays with everyone and gets clean at the same time, which was the only deal in town all along.
stories.notes: mixed age: the Rub-A-Dub Clean Club number plays 2-4; digging in when everyone says the same thing, and the friend who helps anyway, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'ready to find some answers' is the other story; tags anchor on segment_title plus the script. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Someone is making messes around Sagoville, and Harvey and Jack are ready to find some answers! Blueberry Monster makes her debut.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harvey comes out of tag one giant mud splat, and playtime closes everywhere he goes: too muddy for Jinja, for Jack, for tea parties, for swinging. He would rather search the whole town than take a bath, and the search ends with nobody to play with and a very clean-looking forever alone. Robin quietly starts helping him wash, and the friends reroute the whole argument into a Good-Time Rub-A-Dub Clean Club party, where getting clean is the game.

stories.situation: The first-ever camping trip is planned by a dog who packed squeaky toys, a flag, and lots of underwear, and a rabbit who packed carrots. Campsite 4 is real and so is the dark, and there is no flashlight, tent, or sleeping bag in either backpack.
stories.coping: Larry the Log teaches the whole fix in one line, you did not bring it, but you can wing it: a branch becomes a shovel, an empty backpack becomes a sleeping bag, toilet paper becomes a pillow, and a carrot becomes a campfire. The trip they almost skipped becomes the best one yet.
stories.notes: mixed age: the wing-it song plays 2-4; the gap between the camping trip you imagined and the one you can actually have, closed by imagination, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Larry the Log helps Harvey and Jack with their camping trip' omits the packing-list comedy and that every missing supply gets reimagined on the spot. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Larry the Log helps Harvey and Jack with their camping trip. Harvey, Jinja, and Jack try to cheer up Robin.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harvey and Jack arrive at their first campsite with flag, squeaky toys, underwear, and carrots, and discover they brought none of the things camping needs. Going home looks certain until Larry the Log reframes the whole trip: anything at all is just a thing, and the forest provides the rest if you wing it. Stick-shovel, backpack-bed, rainbow bench, carrot campfire, and the unprepared campers have the coziest night in Sagoville.

stories.situation: Robin has a sore wing and has to stay inside, and her friends keep failing to cheer her: the comic book hole is buried in snow, and the Boingy Bear snow statue they build slides off down the hill the moment it is finished. Boingy Bear cannot save anyone from the window Robin watches from.
stories.coping: Nobody fakes the fix: the snow bear runs off and the friends say so, no, we do not have anything to cheer up Robin now. But the runaway statue did save a snow cone and block a snowball on its way, Robin saw her hero be a hero from her window, and the dress-up Boingy Bear show finishes the job inside.

stories.situation: Mr. Stickles, the very best fetching stick, tastes wrong and is a lot less fetch-y, because he is Peanuts' magic wand. The swap has magic words in it: any word but abraca-blooey causes trouble, and the trouble multiplies with every guess, flying pizzas, extra shoes, pigs, then flying blue pigs.
stories.coping: Harvey keeps trying long after the guesses run out, remembers the real magic word mid-chaos, and stops the wand. The apology is a cleanup, wand, fix all the trouble we caused, and ends with both treasures back where they belong, plus wigs for everyone at the show.

stories.situation: Harvey surprises his friends with roller skates and helmets, and Jinja keeps falling before the very first glide. She sits the skating out, I do not think I will ever be able to roller-skate, and decides to watch from the sidelines instead.
stories.coping: The lessons go straight, turn, stop, and the stopping never quite stops. Then Harvey gets stuck in a cloud and Jinja skates a full rescue without falling once, straight, turn, stop, everything she learned, at speed, and the skirt of the pond sees she has been skating the whole time.
stories.notes: mixed age: the skate lessons play 2-4; learning that will not stick until it suddenly does, and courage found mid-rescue, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Harvey, Jack and Robin attend magic training' is the other story; tags anchor on segment_title plus the script. confidence high.

stories.episodeTitle: Turkey Tea Party / Jinja's Mystery Package
stories.situation: Robin's turkey tea party runs on rules: dress like a turkey, curtsy like a turkey, say the gobble words, and only then, tea. The rules are tickly, twirly, and dizzy-making, and her friends start to wobble between wanting tea and wanting to keep their dignity.
stories.coping: Nobody sneaks out and nobody mocks the rules: they ask for a different way in, and Robin says yes each time, own costumes, own curtsies, best-effort gobbles. Robin decides the new version is more silly, and turkeys arrive to a party that fits everyone.
stories.notes: mixed age: the gobble song plays 2-4; a host learning her rules can flex without breaking, and guests asking instead of quitting, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Robin hosts a one-of-a-kind celebration' omits the three rule-adjustment negotiations that are the whole story. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Robin hosts a one-of-a-kind celebration. Harvey leaps into action to save Jinja's surprise from being spoiled.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Robin's turkey tea party has rules, and the rules have opinions: turkey costumes tickle, turkey curtsies cause vertigo, and Harvey's gobble keeps coming out bark. One asked-for change at a time, the party reshapes around the friends instead of losing them, and Robin declares the silly version the best version, with actual turkeys joining the tea.

stories.situation: Harvey peeks at Jinja's mystery package and cannot unpeek: a pretend palm tree escapes its box, the box is ripped, and the surprise he promised not to ruin is standing in the yard in plain sight of a returning Jinja.
stories.coping: Harvey does not shrug, he engineers: a new box from Jack's collection, a failed squish, a costume disguise that fools nobody, and finally wrapping paper, wrapping the whole gang included. Jinja is more surprised than the original plan could have managed, and spends her surprise on a beach party for them.
stories.notes: mixed age: the dress-up-tree gags play 2-4; protecting a surprise for someone else, and the lengths that cost, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'save Jinja's surprise from being spoiled' hides that Harvey caused the spoil-risk by peeking, and that the fix wraps him inside the package. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Robin hosts a one-of-a-kind celebration. Harvey leaps into action to save Jinja's surprise from being spoiled.

stories.situation: Jack's digging for collection space uncovers an underground train station and a mole named Nola building track to the beach. The friends lay rails, the whole town requests stops, and the maiden ride overflows: the train is too small for everyone who helped build it.
stories.coping: The too-small train becomes a puzzle instead of a verdict, and Jack's collections supply the answer, wheels under everything you can sit on, rainbow seat belts included. Everyone rides, including Nola, and the train that went to the beach now goes all over Sagoville.
stories.notes: mixed age: the chugga-chugga numbers play 2-4; building something together and then making room for every builder, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'an underground train sparks excitement' omits Nola, the too-small-train problem, and that the fix comes from Jack's collections. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: An underground train sparks excitement across Sagoville. Rosie and friends help Harvey with a gift delivery.
stories.perStorySynopsis: A dig for storage room turns into a discovered train station, and Harvey and Jack end up laying track beside Nola the train mole, to the beach, the forest, the market, and the mountaintop. The celebration hit is the seating chart: more builders than seats. Jack's collections turn every ridable object into rolling stock, and the Sagoville choo choo departs with the entire construction crew aboard.

stories.situation: Harvey wants to send Grandpa Jasper his saved snowball, a very special delivery, and the sun has other plans. The gift shrinks at every stop on Rosie's route, mittens, shade, tunnels, and umbrellas notwithstanding, and the last leg is pure sunlight with no cover left.
stories.coping: Harvey solves the unfixable by mail: he writes the sun a polite letter asking for shade, and the sun obliges. The snowball arrives small and the gift lands big, because it turns out Grandpa Jasper needed exactly that for lemonade.
stories.notes: mixed age: the shade-chase plays 2-4; a gift losing its grandness in transit and still arriving as love, plus writing to the sun, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'help Harvey with a gift delivery' omits the melt race across four friends' deliveries and the letter to the sun. confidence high.

stories.episodeTitle: A New Boo Boo / Harvey Rocks
stories.situation: Boo Boo the ghost leaves town to visit his grandma, and Harvey volunteer-fills the surpriser job in a bedsheet. Every boo lands flat: friends see him coming, the floating envelope is just his hand, and Remy's superstrong hiccups need a scare Harvey cannot scare.
stories.coping: Harvey keeps adjusting instead of quitting, hiding behind books, popping up unseen, until Dennis laughs anyway, you saw me and you still surprised me. When his own tricks cannot fix Remy's hiccups, he says so, and Boo Boo's return with ghost friends finishes the job.
stories.notes: mixed age: the hiccup gags play 2-4; trying to copy someone else's magic, and learning your own version counts, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'fills in for everyone's favorite prankster' omits the flat-boo failure streak, Dennis's grace note, and the honest handoff when the hiccups outmatch him. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Harvey fills in for everyone's favorite prankster. After adopting a houseful of pet rocks, Harvey realizes he may need some help.
stories.perStorySynopsis: With Boo Boo the ghost away, Harvey borrows the surpriser job and discovers it is harder in a bedsheet: everyone sees him, nothing floats, and Remy's superstrong hiccups shrug off every boo. A pizza-restaurant surprise he is sure failed gets a laugh anyway, and when the hiccups finally need the real ghost, Harvey says so. Boo Boo returns with reinforcements, the hiccups surrender, and the fill-in learns his own kind of surprise counts.

stories.situation: A friendly rock with a tail follows Harvey home and becomes Fluffy, the pet rock, feeding time, belly rubs, rock music and all. Then the whole forest follows, and Harvey's house fills with pets he loves and cannot possibly care for alone, baths, walks, and mop required.
stories.coping: Harvey says the sentence pet owners dread, I love them and I really want to take care of them all, but I am not sure I can do it by myself, and the answer is not returning them, it is sharing: each rock leaves for a friend's home, every rock gets a great friend, every friend gets the perfect pet.
stories.notes: mixed age: rock-bath slapstick plays 2-4; the difference between loving something and being able to care for it, and sharing as the loving answer, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a houseful of pet rocks' omits Fluffy's solo adoption arc, the overload spiral, and that the rocks are rehomed by personality match. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Harvey fills in for everyone's favorite prankster. After adopting a houseful of pet rocks, Harvey realizes he may need some help.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harvey adopts a tail-wagging pet rock named Fluffy, and the whole forest wants in: one rock becomes a houseful of Mittens, Marshmallow, Pooky-Bear, Shaggy Dave, and Puddles, with bath time to prove it. The fun tips over into too much, and Harvey, who wanted to do it all, says out loud that he cannot do it alone. The rehoming that follows is not giving up, it is matching every rock with the right friend, and the whole crew plays fetch together by the end.

stories.situation: Hugbot, the town's hug distributor, goes strange: no hugs, only hopping, huggit, huggit, and a fly-chasing sprint nobody can catch. Every friend who needs a comfort hug after a tumble gets a bounce instead, and worry spreads through Sagoville.
stories.coping: Robin names the goal before the panic wins, if we do not help, Hugbot will never hug again, and hugging is Hugbot's favorite thing. The clue is a ribbit, and the answer is the tool Hugbot taught them: one group hug, the biggest and group-iest ever, pops the frog out gently.
stories.notes: mixed age: the huggit chase plays 2-4; a friend acting strangely needs help, not judgment, and the fix is meeting them the way they help you, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a change in personality' hides the frog reveal, the failed boingy-chase, and that the rescue is a giant hug. confidence high.

Impossible chases and stuck doors lose to the town's own medicine, one enormous group hug that frees the frog and returns the hugs.

stories.episodeTitle: Prize Bow Tie / Bread is Sleeping
stories.situation: Jack needs one orange bow tie to complete his collection, and the carnival's ball game keeps handing the prizes to everyone else. Three tickets, three misses, and a string of near winners while Jack's fun quietly drains out of the day.
stories.coping: Harvey asks the question that matters, are you having any fun, and buys Jack back some joy before the last ticket. The final roll is played for fun, the miss is hilarious instead of heartbreaking, and an orange flag picked up on the way out completes the collection anyway.
stories.notes: mixed age: the carnival games play 2-4; wanting a thing so much it eats the fun, and what Harvey does about it, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'sets his sights on winning a unique prize' omits the three misses, the fun-check intervention, and the flag ending. confidence high.

stories.coping: After every plan fails, the friends name the pattern out loud, all our ideas turn out noisy, and try the one thing left: the quiet game. Bread wakes up happy instead of cranky, thanked by name, and the noise starts fresh on schedule.

stories.coping: Harvey admits mid-game that his tail cannot stop, and Jinja flips the flaw: follow the wag, slow it down, and hide where a slow wag reads as scenery. The pair outlasts the whole seek team, and the tail that tattled becomes the strategy.
stories.notes: mixed age: the ninja training numbers play 2-4; a body part that will not obey, and turning the quirk into the trick, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'helps Harvey stop his tail from wagging' omits the training montage, the game-day failure, and that the ending works because the wag stays. confidence high.

stories.coping: Alan says the regret out loud, I know I said you could keep it, but I miss it very much, and Miles hears him. The rainbow mustache Alan never wanted becomes Miles's best ever, and the old mustache goes home to the face that twirls it.

stories.coping: Robin fixes every problem herself by changing the game instead of the player: stroller skiing, a baby race invented on the spot. The pretend holds all the way to a crawling diaper race that Baby Harvey wins, and nobody had to stop being small to keep playing.

Robin, holding the mommy role, chooses imagination over rules each time, a stroller that skis, a baby race invented for her friend, and the pretend grows bigger instead of ending.

stories.situation: Dewey the water droplet wants to splash with Harvey, and every splash lands on someone who did not sign up: Jinja's book, Ducky's wig, Gary's rainbow, a floating mustache. Harvey's promise to a new friend keeps colliding with everyone else's dry things.
stories.coping: Harvey learns the question that unlocks the whole town, may we splash here, please, and learns that not everybody wants to be wet. Fins supplies the splash philosophy and the sea, and the friends who got splashed show up at the beach once their own stuff was finished.
stories.notes: mixed age: the splash gags play 2-4; enthusiasm that keeps colliding with other people's boundaries, and asking before the wave, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a darling water droplet needs help finding a good place to splash' hides the consent song structure and the friends' late arrival at the beach. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Robin inspires Harvey to play pretend. Dewey, a darling water droplet, needs help finding a good place to splash.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Harvey makes a friend made of water, and their friendship is one splash-width too wide for every place in Sagoville: books get soaked, wigs wilt, mustaches float away. The turn is a question, may we splash here, please, asked at sprinklers, tubs, and finally the sea. The beach works, and the splashed-upon friends arrive on their own schedule to join in.

stories.episodeTitle: A Little Fun / Toothbrush in Space
stories.situation: Harvey and Jinja are too big for the Squeakettes' birthday party games, watching the fun from outside it. Asking for a shrink spell is the ask-for-help move, and it comes with a catch: the magic only lasts a little while.
stories.coping: Being small opens a whole world of play, teapot slides and graham-cracker dancing, and when the magic wears off they are happy to be big again. The song lands the point: seeing things from a small point of view is worth the trip either way.

stories.situation: Jupiter has a problem that will not smile: space broccoli, stuck between planet-sized teeth. The fix needs a toothbrush the size of a sign, a rocket conversion, and one floss improvisation when the broccoli refuses to brush loose.
stories.coping: When brushing fails, Harvey and Larry do not pack up, they wing it, asking a passing space thingy for string. The floss frees the broccoli, the smile returns, and the toothpaste rocket heads home with the job done.

stories.episodeTitle: Listen to the Shoe / Harvey Comes Undone
stories.situation: A beach shoe plays music with no visible reason, and Binky's why has no bottom: guesses are not enough, and nobody actually knows. The scientific method arrives in preschool clothing, wash the sand out, check for an on button, and Juggo's shoe lore supplies the real clue, special shoes only work in pairs.
stories.coping: Nobody fakes an answer to the why: the friends stay curious, test one idea at a time, and follow the music back to the beach where the matching shoe waits in the sand. The mystery ends in a shoe duet owned by Cookie, with everyone invited to the concert.
stories.notes: mixed age: the dancing shoe gags play 2-4; curiosity as a method, guessing as a beginning not an ending, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'make music with an unlikely instrument' omits the full mystery structure and the pair-of-shoes reveal. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Jack, Harvey, and Binky make music with an unlikely instrument. Harvey's sweater unravels all over Sagoville.

stories.situation: Wilson knits Harvey the biggest, coziest sweater in Sagoville history, and Harvey loves it past the point of sense: nothing in the world could make him take it off. Then the sweater unravels mid-walk, and the yarn turns up one strand at a time in everyone else's projects.
stories.coping: Harvey tells Wilson the truth, you worked so hard and now my sweater is just yarn, and gives away strand after strand to Larry's web and Gary's jump rope because they make people happy. There is not enough left for a sweater, so Wilson knits the yarn that remains into a tail cozy, small, and exactly right.
stories.notes: mixed age: the yarn trail plays 2-4; losing a gift, generosity that costs something, and the smaller gift that fits, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Harvey's sweater unravels all over Sagoville' omits that Harvey chooses to let the yarn go piece by piece, and the tail-cozy ending. confidence high.

stories.episodeTitle: Looking for Acorns / Rainbow Wishing Star
stories.situation: Nutmeg's acorn-powered plane needs her buried stash, and the treasure map of dance steps ends directly under the brand new snow castle that Robin and Harvey have not even played with yet. Pushing fails, Remy's snow boat tow cracks the towers, and the mission stalls between a friend's flight and a friend's castle.
stories.coping: Robin invents the compromise nobody thought of, smoosh the castle, play with it and wreck it in the same jump. The acorns surface, Nutmeg fuels up, and the whole crew rides to the mountain where her cousin has built a snow tube ride.
stories.notes: mixed age: the smoosh game plays 2-4; a want colliding with a want, solved by play instead of sacrifice, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'accidentally bury Nutmeg's acorn stash' omits the failed towing, the wreck-or-wait dilemma, and the smoosh-the-castle solution. confidence high.

stories.coping: Harvey fills every stripe with other people's wishes until one remains, and the friends insist the last one is his. Looking at the empty patch of sky where the star came from, he finally knows: wish it home.

stories.coping: Nobody drops their own job to pitch in; each helper adds a link, Kiki plays the banjo so Neville can hold the hat so Harvey can feed Wilson, and the booties win the race against the snow. Wilson's thank-you is booties for everyone.
stories.notes: mixed age: the helper-chain song plays 2-4; how a favor for a friend ripples into a whole town helping, and hands busy with love needing hands, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Wilson works hard on a cozy knitting project' omits the entire chain-of-helpers structure, which is the segment. confidence high.

stories.coping: Harvey rebuilds the pool around the complaints instead of the complaints around the pool, more leaves, shallower spots, a hot tub, a fountain. Even the leaf-blowing clouds get asked what they want, and end up flopping in.

stories.perStorySynopsis: Miles invites Harvey swimming in a pool that is entirely leaves, and the leaf pool party that follows is a masterclass in no: too chilly, too deep, too small, for different friends for different reasons. Harvey widens, warms, and shallows the pool until everyone has a way in, and when the leaf-blowing clouds threaten the whole thing, they get invited in too. Leaf flop.

stories.episodeTitle: Square's Very Kind Gesture / The Eclipse
stories.situation: Square finds two rare bananas on his tree and decides to give one to Circle, but the plan is really about hearing himself called generous. The handoff keeps going wrong: Circle gives one banana away to Triangle, Triangle keeps passing them back, and Square never gets the moment he rehearsed.
stories.coping: Square names the stack of feelings out loud, mad about the plan, then bad about the mad, then sad about that. He keeps the friendship going anyway, admits he wishes he could get it right, and finally gets his thank you at Friday Fun Night, earning the credit honestly.
stories.notes: mixed age: banana comedy and the friendship rituals play 2-4; wanting recognition for a kind act, and feeling bad about feeling mad, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'makes a mistake while sharing rare bananas' hides the rehearsed-speech comedy, the banana ping-pong between friends, and the named feelings stack. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Square makes a mistake while sharing rare bananas. Triangle and Square attempt to keep a secret from Circle.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Square's banana tree sprouts two of the island's most precious fruit, and he plans a gesture worthy of the legend of Square the Generous. But generosity performed for applause keeps misfiring: Circle adores the gift and hands one to Triangle, Triangle finds bananas disgusting but eats one to be polite, and Square's big moment turns into a very polite no thanks. Square confesses the whole scheme to his window light and vows to wait for the tree to sprout again, until a picnic invitation finally gets the thank you right.

stories.episodeTitle: Square's Very Kind Gesture / The Eclipse
stories.situation: Square and Triangle see the moon turn red during Friday Fun Night while Circle is out, and decide it is the one thing that happened without her. Keeping a secret from the shape who knows everything feels thrilling at first, then heavy: Circle starts wearing a box to hide while she confesses, and everyone's secret leaks within a day.
stories.coping: Circle owns her feeling instead of dressing it up as knowledge: she admits she was jealous of the one thing her friends knew first. Square rebuilds the red moon with a lantern so all three share it, turning a secret into a club with Circle in it.
stories.notes: synonym note: feeling left out maps to lonely. mixed age: the secret-keeping slapstick plays 2-4; being the one who knows less than everyone, and confessing envy, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'attempt to keep a secret from Circle' omits the three-way secret leak, Circle's box disguise confession, and that Circle already knew it was an eclipse all along. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Square makes a mistake while sharing rare bananas. Triangle and Square attempt to keep a secret from Circle.
stories.perStorySynopsis: When the moon turns red the night Circle misses Friday Fun Night, Square and Triangle decide to keep the eclipse as their own chosen-by-the-moon secret. The not-telling eats at everyone: Square cracks first, wearing a box to confess to Circle, then Triangle spills his own giant-with-a-marker version, and Circle finally snaps that she has been quietly jealous of the one mystery that got past her. She explains the real science of a lunar eclipse, then re-creates it with a lantern so all three shapes see the red moon together.

stories.situation: Winter strips Square of kites, beaches, and apple picking, and he goes quiet and gray with it. Circle and Triangle invent Yeti Night, a made-up holiday about a muffin-sniffing yeti who roars spring awake, and keep the loving lie running for years, until Square catches them mid-impression and learns the magic was homemade.
stories.coping: The friends confess the whole invention when the truth comes out, and own that they kept it up because the magic was working. Square's winter still hurts, but he carries Yeti Night with him, magic made from scratch, and teaches a very real, very shy yeti the part where you roar.
stories.notes: emoji note: muffin ideas swapped for a coat-and-smile set, keep simple. mixed age: the yeti hunt and snow gags play 2-4; the winter blues themselves, a well-meant lie from friends, and rebuilding trust on a frozen mountain, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'creating a new holiday' hides that the yeti turns out real, that Square briefly moves to the woods, and that the ending hands the holiday to the yeti herself. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: The chilly season leaves Square feeling sad, so Circle and Triangle try to cheer him up by creating a new holiday.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Square cannot remember what spring feels like, so his friends invent a holiday about a yeti whose roar wakes the season, muffins in apricot preserves and all. Years of footprints, fake fur, and doorstep muffin thefts later, Square catches them red-handed and the magic cracks: the yeti was never real, and neither were the traditions he loved best. Then a frozen mountain, an enormous footprint, and an actual yeti too shy to leave her cave give the story back its ending, because winter feels less gloomy when you make the magic from scratch, and even the bleakest winters end.

stories.episodeTitle: Square's Big Prank / Circle's Plan Falls Apart
stories.situation: Triangle pranks Square every single morning, and Square decides it has gone on too long: he will pull one prank so big Triangle never pranks him again. Every attempt bounces off, the moved mug goes unnoticed, the boot-tying makes no dent, the turtle in the bed becomes Triangle's new best friend, and Circle keeps telling him to go bigger.
stories.coping: Square stops accepting advice that does not fit and goes with his own enormous idea, moving Triangle's whole house. It backfires into friendship: Triangle is awed, and the two agree to a prank war, which is not the stopping Square wanted but is a way to play as equals.
stories.notes: mixed age: turtle-in-the-bed and house-moving slapstick plays 2-4; the escalation spiral, where trying to win makes the game bigger, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'plans a sneaky surprise' hides the unprankable-Triangle gag ladder and that the huge prank destroys a house and is rewarded. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Eager to outwit Triangle, Square plans a sneaky surprise. Circle searches for answers when a critter kidnaps her plant.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Every morning Triangle shouts gotcha and Square eats breakfast mid-prank, until Square decides the war ends today. He sneaks, he moves mugs, he plants a turtle, and nothing lands: Triangle is unprankable and keeps getting better advice from Circle, go bigger, then huge, then enormous. So Square goes enormous, and shoves Triangle's whole house across the island. Triangle is thrilled, a prank war is declared, and Square learns the hard way that winning at pranks means they never stop.

stories.situation: Circle has tended one plant for a hundred years, and today, at last, it blooms. Then a small critter snatches the whole pot and bolts, and Circle chases it far from home, shouting at it to answer her, until she is somewhere she has never been with no plant and no plan.
stories.coping: Circle says exactly what she has lost and why it hurts, and when the chase leaves her stranded the island answers her instead: wildflowers bloom all around her, and she lets the day be about that gift rather than the ruined plan.
stories.notes: mixed age: the critter chase plays 2-4; losing the one thing you waited a hundred years for, and being okay anyway, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a critter kidnaps her plant' is the spine; the script adds the century of daily care and the wild bloom payoff that the synopsis never mentions. confidence high.

Then she looks around: the wild ones, the flowers nobody planted or planned, bloom for her exactly where she stands.

stories.episodeTitle: Triangle Gets Carried Away / Square's Different Day
stories.situation: Tired of dunking his own doughnuts, Triangle builds a doughnut-dunking machine, and it snowballs into a giant, faulty, copy-everything contraption with a controller helmet. When it grabs him and runs wild, he refuses to tell Circle, because she will say the thing he cannot bear to hear: that he got carried away.
stories.coping: Triangle admits it himself, out loud, before anyone else can: he got carried away, and then he asks Circle for the one favor he refused all day, to find the switch and turn the machine off. Her rescue turns the wreck into the friends' new morning spot.
stories.notes: mixed age: the runaway machine dunking Square's mug is 2-4 comedy; not wanting help because the truth sounds like a criticism lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a simple plan leads to an enormous project' skips the fear of being told I told you so as the real obstacle, and that the machine ends as a picnic island. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: A simple plan leads to an enormous project for Triangle. Square works on a sculpture of Circle.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Triangle's answer to doughnut-dunking drudgery is one small machine, which becomes a huge machine, which becomes a monster with a controller helmet that copies his every move and then ignores them. He would rather ride a berserk doughnut dunker across the island than say Circle was right, but halfway through the sky he says it anyway. She takes the controls, the dunking stops, and the wreckage settles into the best doughnut spot on the island.

stories.situation: Square pushes the same block up the same hill every day, until Circle mistakes him for a genius sculptor and orders a perfect sculpture of herself by tomorrow. He has never sculpted anything. He carves the whole block to nothing, plans to hide in his cave forever, and when she shows up early he says the work is finished when it is not.
stories.coping: Circle reframes the pile of rubble as the sculpture, beguiling and exactly her, and Square lets the kind reading stand. The mistake he wanted to bury becomes the thing she loves.
stories.notes: mixed age: block-pushing routines play 2-4; perfectionism, the wish to hide from a letdown, and the tiny lie that tries to cover it, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Square works on a sculpture of Circle' omits the total destruction of the block, the plan to live underground with the worms, and Circle's generous reframe. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: A simple plan leads to an enormous project for Triangle. Square works on a sculpture of Circle.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Square's days are identical by design, block up the hill, block on the pile, until Circle calls the result a masterpiece of herself and promises to collect it tomorrow. She looks at the rubble and sees a beguiling sculpture of exactly who she is, and Square lets himself be a genius after all.

stories.situation: Triangle announces Triangle Day, a holiday nobody has heard of, and drags Square and Circle through gift giving, a sacred dance, a triangle song, and repeated marches up the mountain. They suspect a prank the whole time and nearly quit at tradition four, until Triangle explains what the day actually is: the one day a year he gets to be fully himself.
stories.coping: Square and Circle hang in past the point of doubt and let Triangle explain the day in his own words, loud energy and accidental breakage included. Hearing what it means to him turns suspicion into celebration, and they wish it did not have to end.
stories.notes: mixed age: the silly traditions and the mountain slogs play 2-4; honoring a friend's difference when their energy is hard to match, and staying through the doubt, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'learn how to celebrate a unique holiday' hides the prank suspicion, the exhausting tradition ladder, and Triangle's quiet closing admission that being fully him is hard for his friends sometimes. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Circle and Square learn how to celebrate a unique holiday. An approaching storm excites Triangle and worries his friends.

Instead Triangle tells them the truth: the day is the one day he gets to be fully himself, and sharing it with the only two friends he has matters more than the traditions. Then the sun unlocks the triangle door, and the last part of Triangle Day is his alone.

stories.coping: The trick is not a lecture, it is a galactic board game and a warm cup: Triangle gets absorbed turn by turn and forgets the show he was missing. He still declares he is going back out, but one more cup and one more game keep him exactly where it is safe.
stories.notes: vibe note: felt energy is high early with a cozy settle at the end. mixed age: storm spectacle and the game subplot play 2-4; naming why the storm tempts him, and being drawn in by warmth rather than rules, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'excites Triangle and worries his friends' skips the hot chocolate delay, Stellar Chronicles, and the ending where he never actually goes back out. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Circle and Square learn how to celebrate a unique holiday. An approaching storm excites Triangle and worries his friends.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Triangle checks the wind, the pressure, and his deep sense of unease, and declares the coming storm a must-see show worth a tree-side seat. Circle and Square haul him into the designated safety zone, where the hot chocolate takes forever and a board game called Stellar Chronicles waits. One token turn at a time, the spectacle he came for loses to a character with spikes and lasers who looks just like him, and by the time his cup is poured, the storm outside is the thing he is missing.

stories.episodeTitle: Message in a Bottle / Square's Special Place
stories.situation: On beach tidying day Square finds notes in bottles that know his pancake secrets, and he and Triangle spiral into a spy panic, wire their house against imaginary bugs, and dig a trap hole. The spy is Circle, who writes her private thoughts into bottles and drops them in the ocean to let them drift away, and her two friends have now read them twice.
stories.coping: Circle explains what the bottles really were, a way to sort foggy feelings and watch them drift off, and Square and Triangle own the reading outright with a pinkie promise. When they break it anyway and get caught, the apology is harder and more honest: we are terrible friends, we cannot believe us either.
stories.notes: mixed age: the spy-trap slapstick plays 2-4; reading someone's private writing, the pinkie promise broken twice, and earning trust back, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'mysterious bottles on the beach' hides the full spy conspiracy arc and that Circle's coping ritual, not any secret, is what the bottles hold. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Triangle and Square find mysterious bottles on the beach. While playing hide-and-seek, Square discovers a peaceful spot that is just his.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Notes washed up by the storm know things only a spy could know: the cinnamon in Square's pancakes, Triangle's sleep talk, a borrowed yo-yo. The two build a counter-surveillance operation with disguises and a trap hole, and catch exactly one person: Circle, whose private ritual is writing her thoughts into bottles and giving them to the ocean. Twice her friends pry into what she meant to let drift away, and twice the apology has to grow, from pinkie promise to the plain confession that there is no believing them left to do.

stories.episodeTitle: Message in a Bottle / Square's Special Place
stories.situation: Mid-game, Square finds a hollow that fits him exactly, a quiet place of soft bark and embroidered corners that is all his own. Then Triangle and Square's friends wander in, admire the decor, evict the ants, and decide it could be their place, and Square stops coming back.
stories.coping: Square never makes a speech about it; the story lets him keep the place the only way it can be kept after it changes, in memory and in returning to it inside himself whenever the day gets loud. The friends' love is real and still costs him something.
stories.notes: situation note: no starter vocabulary fits, written as needing a special place of one's own, propose addition for vocabulary review. mixed age: hide-and-seek plays 2-4; the bittersweet lesson that sharing a private place changes it, and that you carry it with you, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'discovers a peaceful spot' omits the friends taking it over and the long quiet afterward. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Triangle and Square find mysterious bottles on the beach. While playing hide-and-seek, Square discovers a peaceful spot that is just his.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Square is losing at shroud-and-find when he drops into a hollow that feels made for him, and something in him goes quiet and glad. He keeps coming back, until his friends find it too, furnish it with compliments and ant removal, and call it their place. After that Square does not return any time soon or any time later, and the story closes on what the hollow taught him: you can always go back to your special place, even if you are not there.

stories.episodeTitle: Triangle Goes Solo / Circle Makes a Mistake
stories.situation: Triangle heads into the wild alone to find his true self, unshackled from the crowd of two, with a feather in his cap and no audience. The adventure delivers snakes and deserts, but every triumph goes unapplauded, and he starts narrating to a rock named Rocko.
stories.coping: Triangle never admits the ache directly; he replaces it, naming a rock so there is someone to tell. When Square and Circle confess they followed him out of worry, he gets his audience back and lights up, and only checks that nobody saw the rock conversations.
stories.notes: mixed age: Rocko and the snake stories play 2-4; the question of who an accomplishment is for, when no one is watching, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'sets out on his own' omits the invented audience, the lost-supplies collapse, and that the friends secretly shadowed the whole trip. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: The fearless Triangle sets out on his own. Circle leads a journey to ancient ruins and unexpectedly runs into trouble.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Triangle declares independence from the expectations of the crowd, meaning Square and Circle, and sets off to wrestle beasts and discover himself. Alone under an indifferent sky, his feats pile up with no one to tell, so he adopts a rock called Rocko and feeds him ghost stories and achievements alike. It takes losing his supplies to say what the trip was really missing, and just then the truth arrives: his friends followed him the whole way, worried, and Triangle the Great Adventurer gets his audience after all.

stories.episodeTitle: Triangle Goes Solo / Circle Makes a Mistake
stories.situation: Circle, the shape who is never wrong, leads her friends to the ancient ruins and forgets two things they cannot do: hover, and outrun a tide. Stranded overnight with no chamomile, no turtle to tuck in, and a boat plan that collapses, she blames Square, then Triangle, then the berries, before the truth lands on her.
stories.coping: Circle says the plain sentence nobody expected from her: it is my fault, I was thinking about myself, and I owe you an apology. Square and Triangle answer with trust instead of a grudge and stories of their own disasters instead of a score.
stories.notes: mixed age: the stranding comedy plays 2-4; the always-right friend making a real mistake and being forgiven, and forgiving herself, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'unexpectedly runs into trouble' hides the blame chain, the crust-eating, and that Circle's apology is the first fault she has ever claimed. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: The fearless Triangle sets out on his own. Circle leads a journey to ancient ruins and unexpectedly runs into trouble.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Circle plans the perfect adventure to the ancient ruins, and the plan dissolves when the tide covers the only path home and her friends, who cannot hover, are stuck. The blame bounces: Square's slowness, Triangle's berry-snacking, Mother Nature herself, until Circle runs out of places to put it. For the first time she owns a mistake out loud, apologizes, and learns that the friends who always mess up are also the friends who always trust, and never keep the ledger.

stories.situation: Square has planned every second of the best sleepover ever, puzzle by timed puzzle, and his guests keep wanting other things: one ghost story, then another, then a pillow fort. Each detour puts him further behind schedule until he is marching off for the box of natural fibers, and the hurt comes out at last: I planned this so carefully, and all you want to do is what you want to do.
stories.coping: Square names what is really hurting, that his idea of fun and his friends' idea have split, and they hear him. The schedule dissolves into an unscheduled pillow fight, and the sleepover that broke the plan turns out better than the plan.
stories.notes: mixed age: ghost stories and the pillow fight play 2-4; the planner learning that fun cannot be scheduled into a friend, and saying why he is upset, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a change of plans tests Square's patience' hides the timed-puzzle regime, the 30-second ghost story cutoff, and the honest fight that saves the night. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: A change of plans tests Square's patience. Circle helps Square start a garden, but she struggles with his instructions.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Square has spent months scheduling maximum fun: puzzle, puzzle, bigger puzzle, lemon bars. His guests would rather tell ghost stories, get scared by one, and build a pillow fort, and every detour costs his timeline thirty seconds it cannot spare. When he storms off for basket weaving, the real reason spills out, that nobody wants what he planned, and the friends he invited answer by throwing the first pillow. The sleepover nobody stuck to the agenda for is the best one yet.

stories.situation: Circle teaches Square to garden, and his first-ever plot comes up greener and juicier than her own. Everyone keeps agreeing his garden is wonderful, and the teacher who has done this for years quietly decides there is no point trying anymore.
stories.coping: Triangle's juggling settles it sideways: he has missed every catch for years and does it anyway, because he likes it. Circle picks her cucumbers back up, admits what she was feeling by fixing a salad together, and the two gardens end up on one plate.
stories.notes: mixed age: juggling tomatoes that splat play 2-4; being outshone by someone you taught, and starting again anyway, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'she struggles with his instructions' is backwards to the script, Square blooms, Circle wilts, and the rescue is a joke about splatting tomatoes. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: A change of plans tests Square's patience. Circle helps Square start a garden, but she struggles with his instructions.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Circle takes on her most patient student and Square turns out to be a natural, with melon vines greener than hers and the island wondering about its new master gardener. The teacher keeps congratulating him in a voice that gets smaller each time, then quits over tomatoes for juggling practice. A friend who cannot catch anything after two years, and keeps juggling because it is fun, hands her the wisdom without knowing it, and the patch that failed this year still grows a very good salad.

stories.episodeTitle: Triangle and Square's Big Game / The Shooting Star
stories.situation: Circle watches their jumping game once and calls it silly, and the word unhinges its inventors. If the game is silly, maybe they are, and the two retire from games entirely to sit seriously and look at stuff, until they catch Circle alone, playing her own game of rolling in circles until the world goes weird.
stories.coping: Seeing that even Circle has a game nobody else plays unlocks the thought they needed: it is not for us, and it does not have to be. They stop needing her verdict, pick their own game back up, and race each other to the pine tree.
stories.notes: mixed age: the game slapstick plays 2-4; one person's silly making you question the thing you love, and putting it down again, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'feel insecure' is the spine; the script adds the serious-stuff protest, the dizzy-game discovery, and the it's-not-for-us loop that resolves it. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: When Circle brushes off their game, Triangle and Square feel insecure. A mysterious meteor crash inspires a treasure hunt.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The Leapstravaganza has everything, jumping, leaping, goggles, and one spectator verdict: silly. Triangle and Square take the word home and dissect it until the game they made up feels unsalvageable, then retire to the serious sport of looking at stuff. Catching Circle mid-roll in her own private dizzy game teaches them the thing no pep talk could, that games do not have to be for everyone to be worth playing, and the rematch to the pine tree is on.

stories.episodeTitle: Triangle and Square's Big Game / The Shooting Star
stories.situation: For the first time in 237 years a meteor shower is visible from the island, and one streak appears to land. The three trek across beach, stream, and peak to find it, each telling the story of the falling rock on the way, and the crater at the end holds nothing at all.
stories.coping: Circle had hoped for more than an empty hole and says so when asked, then declares the expedition a success anyway, a rare crater witnessed. Triangle and Square bring the feeling home the reliable way, with a race.
stories.notes: emoji note: crater and nest ideas rejected, kept star, rock, smile. mixed age: the expedition romp plays 2-4; hoping hard for something and finding an empty crater, and calling the trip worth it anyway, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a mysterious meteor crash inspires a treasure hunt' omits the three stories told on the hike and Circle's lonely-space-rock version that quietly explains the ending. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: When Circle brushes off their game, Triangle and Square feel insecure. A mysterious meteor crash inspires a treasure hunt.
stories.perStorySynopsis: A meteor shower arrives for the first time in 237 years, one streak looks like a landing, and the shooting star expedition is on. Three terrains later, with Triangle's fiery-inferno version and Circle's tale of a solitary space rock that slows for a bursting green island, they crest Tall Peak and find only an empty crater. Circle admits she hoped for more, then names the rare crater itself the discovery, and the walk home turns into a race to the pine tree.
